Then, in the same manner, facing inward from behind the curtain, with eyes as steady as the stones of Mount Meru and Mandara, he looked with a gaze of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). With a garland of cool white rays produced by the *svadhā* [mantra] and the syllable *Oṃ*, he established those who had perished—those observing nihilistic vows—in the delusion of the Buddha and in non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*). Thus, at the eastern gate, he appeared white, eternal, and bearing a fabricated discus; likewise, he was endowed with a face turned inward and other such attributes.

With a gaze directed toward the left following the left side, [he says] "Oṃ Vajradṛṣṭi ruṭa mahiti. By means of the hook of light rays from the syllable Hrīḥ of Tārā, he establishes the Śrāvakas and others—who are inclined toward [limited] awakening—within the awakening of great passion. Having impassioned them, he becomes red in color and holds a conventional lotus; he is Narteśvara at the western gate.

Likewise, other yogins should also sever the interval by means of their respective individual natures (*svarūpa*), and without fabricating it with the forms gathered by each individually, they should imagine themselves abiding upon the summit of Mount Meru and perform the dance. When examining that, one should do everything as before at the eastern gate, holding a white-colored, fabricated wheel, and [visualizing] the eye of *Oṃ* and the eyeball.

With a loving gaze, one should look upon those fallen into views that cling to extremist ascetic practices with a garland of cool nectar-like light, intending to establish them in the Buddha’s non-abiding nirvāṇa, free from delusion. Likewise, at the western gate is Padmanarteśvara, red in color, holding an artificial lotus and marked with the syllable *hrīḥ*. *Oṃ vajra...*

Regarding the one called *Dṛṣṭarutāmatā*, imagine that by the light of the lasso of vision resting on the left, those abiding in the enlightenment of the Śrāvakas and others are drawn with longing, and thus they are directed toward the enlightenment of desire (*rāga-bodhi*).

Likewise, at the northern gate is the green supreme horse, equipped with a face such as that of a green horse and so forth, possessing a blazing gaze as his goad; having taken recourse to the path of the Omniscient One, he brings even those who have reached the stages of a Bodhisattva to certainty in perfect enlightenment by displaying various emanations to those who have entered the paths of the Śrāvakas and others through the manifestation of miraculous powers, while holding a simulated sword.

Likewise, at the northern gate, visualize the Supreme Steed of Truth (Paramārtha-haya), green in color, holding a sword with a green hilt and possessing a green horse-head, blazing exactly as it is described. With a gaze that looks upon all things, imagine that by means of a hook, he leads those who have entered the path of the Śrāvakas—such as the Bodhisattvas of Hearing (*śrutavān*) and others—onto the path of omniscience through various emanations.

Likewise, he is endowed with a golden face and so forth; his eyes are wide open and darting, his gaze drawing in the *yakṣīs*. "Oṃ Dīptadṛṣṭyaṅkuśi Jaḥ!"—with the hook of his gaze, whose yellow pupils are directed upward toward the right side of the sun and moon, he removes the envy of the proud and wicked, establishes them in the knowledge of equanimity, and holds a jewel made of precious gems in his hand as Vajrasūrya. He is yellow and resides at the southern gate, according to the statement: "East, west, north, and south."
Likewise, at the southern gate, there is a yellow Vajrasūrya adorned with artificial jewels; [recite]: *Oṃ dīpta-dṛśya āṃ kuśa jaḥ*.

Thus it is said; and one should visualize that by drawing the sun and moon with the right eye and moving them swiftly, the hook of the lotus-eye clears away defects such as envy and the like, and applies [the mind] to the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*). As it is stated: "In the east, west, north, and south directions, they are applied in succession."

All [the deities] have bodies half the size of a night (nīśārdha), wear artificial garments, and possess human ornaments; they have artificial, tawny, blazing hair; they wear crowns consisting of garlands of skulls and the five Buddhas; they stand in the dancing posture with one leg half-crossed (ardhaparyaṅka); they are three-eyed; they stand upon artificial universal lotuses and sun disks; however, Śāśvata has a moon-seat and moon-like radiance.

Every day, she dwells in a dance posture upon an artificial tiger skin garment, with artificial reddish-yellow hair, a crown of the skulls of the five Buddhas, and three eyes; she stands upon various artificial lotuses and sun discs, half-crouched, especially upon a seat of the eternal moon and radiant light.
Likewise, Locanā, white in color and holding an artificial wheel, pacifies the misfortunes and afflictions of sentient beings through her gaze of loving-kindness, residing in the northeast.
Likewise, at the boundary of the northeast, there is the white-eyed Māmakī, holding a jewel-ornamented wheel and gazing with a loving look to protect sentient beings from harm;
similarly, in the southeast corner is the blue Māmakī, whose lotus-like hand holds a jewel-adorned vajra, who strikes down the afflictions of enemy armies with the Vajra-gaze.

Likewise, at the southeast corner (Agni), one should protect those afflicted by enemy armies by holding a blue, artificial vajra with the color of Māmakī and gazing with the "vajra-look. Likewise, at the southwest corner (Nairṛtya), Pāṇḍarā, red in color, holding an artificial lotus,
inspires passion in beings by gazing with the "passionate look."

Likewise, in the northwest corner is Tārā, green in color, holding a blue lotus; with a gaze of attraction, she draws in those to be converted. All of them, as before, have brown hair that stands upright and blazes; they possess artificial eyes, faces, and so forth, which are radiant. Their left hands form the heart-fist with the index finger extended; they wear artificial garments of the universal pattern (*viśva*). They stand in the *pratyālīḍha* posture upon artificial universal-lotus sun-discs, their limbs smeared with gold and ink.

On that day as well, she sat with her left leg extended upon an artificial lotus and sun disc, possessing artificial tawny-yellow hair, an artificial face, and artificial garments; her complexion was altered by pigments, and her left hand formed the threatening mudrā at her heart.

Likewise, he who observes both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa is the one-eyed (kekara) Acala, because he is intent on looking down and up. He holds a sword, a threatening forefinger, and a snake-noose. He is intent on mocking the Cakravartin and his queen. He stands in the pratyālīḍha posture upon a sun disk on a universal lotus. Whirling beside each Cakravartin and queen, he is adorned with various jewels, ornaments, and fine garments. Wearing a crown of jewels with Citteśvara [Avalokiteśvara] at its center, he mocks them.

Likewise, one should contemplate the wrathful Acala, holding a sword, a threatening gesture, and a nāga-foot, standing with his left leg extended upon an artificial lotus and sun disk. Adorned with various ornaments such as jewels and wearing fine garments, he is surrounded by universal monarchs and goddesses who gaze upward and downward, appearing both terrifying and peaceful, and thus contemplate the equality of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) and peace (*śānti*).
On all sides, beginning with the Vajrapada and others, and endowed with the five types of lotus-turnings (*kamalāvarta*) and so forth,
they perform the dance in due order through ninety-eight foot-steps (*akṣepa*).
Singing a song, one should take up the chant there:
"The supreme *puruṣa* is empty, stainless, and by nature like a dream."
Meditate on the nature of the mind; liberation is not attained until it is realized. — Māmakyāḥ.
Until emptiness, the supreme naked essence,
is realized as having the nature of dreams and illusions,
for that long—

One should meditate on the nature of the mind; this is the song of Māmakhī. "Neither in existence nor in nirvāṇa—therein lies that great bliss which is free from [duality]. Whoever contemplates with mental cultivation accomplishes the supreme task. —This is the teaching of Locanā.
That which is neither birth nor nirvana is the great bliss vajra;
for one whose mind has no meditation upon it.
This is the accomplishment of what is to be done; it belongs to Locanā.
Even if deprived of a single syllable, it is neither the *bindu* nor the mind.
This is that supreme great bliss; it is neither removed nor added. [This belongs to] Pāṇḍaravāsī.
Abandoning mantras and letters,
the mind free from bindus and sounds—
that is supreme great bliss.
"In this, there is neither removal nor addition; it is the White-Robed One.
Whatever is the nature of the reflection, that very thing is to be meditated upon as the state of being.
It is empty, stainless, and the supreme fruit; therein there is neither merit nor sin. — Tārāyāḥ.
Just as a reflected image has no inherent nature,
so too should one meditate upon all phenomena;
this is the supreme, naked emptiness.
"Neither merit nor sin exists; this is Tārā’s milk.
That which is neither true nor false in the midst of the water—that body is pure by its very nature within the circle of the maṇḍala. Thus spoke all the assemblies.
Just like the moon reflected in water,
it is neither true nor false;
by means of the supreme mandala wheel, [it is realized].
"The body, too, should be viewed in that same way," thus he spoke to the entire assembly.
"In the theater of the *dharmodaya* city" means: on the stage whose form is the *dharmodaya*.
"In the city of Gar-gyi-grong-khyer, which is the source of phenomena (chos-’byung), the abode of the merchant.

From the *Tattvāloka*, the difficult commentary on the *Vajrapañjara-māhāyoginī-tantra*, this is the explanation of the second chapter.

Regarding the phrase "abiding in the *vajrapañjara* samādhi": it means abiding in the *hevajra* samādhi. Regarding the phrase "one should utter the *mahābhūta* offering": the *mahābhūtas* are the guardians of the directions (*dikpālas*). Their *bali* is the offering for worship (*pūjopahāra*).

"Abiding in the samādhi called 'Vajrapāśa' (Vajra-Net)" means abiding in the samādhi of Hevajra. "One should offer the bali-offering to the great bhūtas" refers to the practice of the bali-offering together with the ritual services for the purpose of satisfying the great bhūtas.
And as it has been said:
"With all ornaments adorning his body, he is adorned with vajra-ornaments."
Taking up the bell and vajra, one should offer the bali-oblation at the four [directions].
One should place flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, conch shells, and so forth on the right;
the mantra-vessel for the *arghya* offering on the left;
and the vessel for the feet (*pādya*) in front, according to the previous procedure, following the sequence of flowers, incense, and the rest.
Having performed worship with flowers and other offerings, one should cause the auspicious [deity] to be seated upon a great seat.
By means of forms that scatter flowers and forms that scatter perfumes,
from the two trees with garlands of lamps, and with ointments, gestures, and fragrances.
Through the *lāsya* gesture and the *lāsya* [song], Mālyaḍākinī [is attained];
through song and the utterances of *hūṃ*, the song [is realized]; and through the contraction of the elbows, the dance [is performed].
For this is the unsurpassed worship that brings satisfaction to the Buddhas.

Furthermore, it is said: "Adorned with all the ornaments of the limbs, beautified by vajra ornaments, and holding a vajra and bell, one should offer the *bali* at the crossroads of the path. To the right, place flowers, incense, lamps, and fragrant conch shells; to the left, the vessel for the mantra-offering water (*argha*). Having placed another vessel in front, first perform the ritual of rinsing the mouth, followed by the flowers and so forth in sequence."

Having performed offerings such as giving alms and presenting flowers, one should offer them into a beautiful vessel. One should move them in the manner of flowers, move them in the manner of incense, lift up lamps, and apply perfumes in the manner of scent. With playful hands, one should act with grace; like a garland of ḍākinīs, one should sing the song beginning with "Hūṃ" and summon [the deities] through the dance with the thumbs. These...

"Blameless offering" means that it pleases the Buddhas. "Situated in the middle of the space-element" means within the *dharmodayā*. "Eight lotuses" means one should visualize an eight-petaled lotus immediately following the meditation on emptiness. "From the syllable *HŪṂ*" means by means of the *HŪṂ* syllables; on the petals in the cardinal and intermediate directions are Indra and the others, black in color. "From the syllable *OṂ*" means by means of the *OṂ* syllables; above are Brahmā and the others, white in color. "From the syllable *ĀḤ*" means by means of the *ĀḤ* syllables; the unnamed *nāgas* residing in the underworld have their bodies embraced by their respective consorts (*svābhavidyā*), with hands holding a vajra and a vajra-bell.

"Abiding in the center of the expanse of space" means having entered into the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*). "Lotus" refers to a red eight-petaled lotus. "To be meditated upon" means following the meditation on emptiness. "From *Hūṃ*" means from the various *Hūṃ*s; on the petals of the cardinal and intermediate directions are Indra and the others, blue in color.

Likewise, the Brahmins and so forth in the upper [direction] should be made white from the syllable Oṃ; the Nagas and so forth in the subterranean regions should be made red from the syllable Āḥ. All of them hold vajra bells and are embraced by their respective consorts.

"Standing in the ālīḍha posture" means upon a sun disc on a universal lotus. "Brahmā and the others" refers to those beginning with Brahmā. "By the eternal one" means by Vairocana. "Indra and the others, by the wielder of the vajra" means by Akṣobhya. "Karkoṭaka and the others, by the lords of dance" means by Amitābha. "All are born from the three families" means they arise from the three syllables whose intrinsic natures are delusion, hatred, and passion.

"Upon the seat with legs extended to the right" refers to the various lotuses and sun disks. "The examination of Brahmā and so forth" refers to Vairocana. "Vajra for Indra and so forth" refers to Akṣobhya. "Lāsya for Karkoṭa and so forth" refers to Amitābha. "All are born from the three families" refers to [the lineage of] Gti... (Maitreya).
The nature of delusion, hatred, and attachment arises from the three syllables.

Regarding "attraction by Gaurī": having generated the *samayasattva* within Gaurī, one performs the attraction of the *jñānasattva*. Having visualized [the deity] with Gaurī’s binding nooses and the *sphoṭabandha*, [one acts] with Ghasmarī for subjugation, [saying] "by the bell. This is easy to understand.

Regarding the phrase "one should summon with the *gaurī*," this refers to summoning the wisdom-wheel (*jñānacakra*) by means of the hook of *gaurī*, following the generation of the commitment-wheel (*samayacakra*). As for the passage beginning with "having inserted it with the foot of *ṭzorī*," it is easy to understand.

Then, having offered the *argha* and *pādya*, one should satisfy [the deities] with this mantra. "Argha" and "pādya" are indicative; having performed the worship and praise, one should produce nectar through [processes such as] flaming and heating, and thereby satisfy them. In rites for pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth, one should satisfy those whose faces are held by white-colored vajras and the like; in rites for killing (*māraṇa*) and so forth, one should satisfy those with wrathful-vajra tongues and faces turned away. The remainder is easy to understand. || o ||

"Then, having offered the arghya and the water for washing the feet, one should satisfy [the deities] with this mantra. Here, "arghya and water for washing the feet" is merely an illustration; one should perform the offerings and praises, purify with the three syllables beginning with *Oṃ*, and transform [the substances] into nectar through the process of heating (*btsos pa*) and so forth. Then, for the peaceful rites and others, one should offer them into the mouths adorned with white vajras and so forth.

The *cung zad* (slightly) and *phyed bar* (halfway) are for the purpose of [distinguishing] the poor; as for killing and so forth, they are to be visualized with a wrathful vajra-adorned face. The remainder is easy to understand.

Within the various lines of the verses, there are names arranged both in their proper and reverse orders; having rectified these very [names], they are explained according to the divisions of the families (*kula*).
In various passages of the treatise, such as the phrase "de nas" (then), the names of the vajras appear to be intermingled; these shall now be arranged in their proper order and explained.

In the Vajra family: Hāsavajra, Padmāṅkuśavajra, Vilāsavajra, Līlāvajra, Anala-vajra. In the Moha family: Jñānavajra, Āveśavajra, Pāramitāvajra, Lalitavajra. In the Rāga family: Suratāṅkuravajra, Padmavajra, Padmāṅkuravajra, Avalokitavajra, Rāgavajra. In the Maṇi family: Cintāmaṇivajra, Anaṅgavajra, Paramānandavajra, Suratānandavajra, Suratavajra. In the Samaya family:
Prajñāvajra, Prajñāṅkuravajra, Karuṇāṅkuravajra, Gaganavajra. || O ||

Vajrahāsa, Vajravikrīḍita, Vajralāsa, and Vajrāla are of the hatred family. Vajrajñāna, Vajrāveśa, and Vajrapāramitā are of the delusion family. Vajra-aṅkura, Vajrapadma, Vajrapadmāṅkura, Vajrasamantadarśana, and Vajra...

The Vajras of Passion belong to the *rāga*-family. The Vajra-Cintāmaṇi, the Vajra-Anaṅga, the Vajra-Paramānanda, the Vajra-Ratimukha, and the Vajra-Rati belong to the *ratna*-family. The Vajra-Prajñā, the Vajra-Prajñāsūtra, the Vajra-Karuṇāsūtra, and the Vajra-Gagana belong to the *samaya*-family.

In the family of Hatred (*dveṣakula*), there are the ḍākinīs: Jñānagarvī, Vajrāstrā, Vajrāhosukhā, Vajranairātmyā, and Vajrakarā. In the family of Delusion (*mohakula*), there are: Vajralocanā, Vajraḍākinī, Vajragaurī, and Vajramāyā. In the family of Jewel (*maṇikula*), there are: Vajrajvālā, Vajralatā, Vajravegā, Vajravetālī, Vajrāṅkuśā, and Vajrāvalī. In the family of Passion (*rāgakula*), there are: Vajramālā, Vajralāsyā, Vajrahāsyā, Vajrāśleṣā, Vajravikacā, Vajrapadmā, and Vajrarāgā.
In the midst of envy: Vajrodayā, Vajravaḍavā, Vajratārā, Vajraghā, Vajravilāsinī, Vajramatī, Vajrakoṅkaṇā, Vajralālā, and Vajraśvāsā.

The ḍākinīs are to be described as follows: Vajragarbha, Vajraśastra, Vajrānandā, Vajranairātmyā, and Vajrabhujā belong to the family of hatred. Vajralocanā, Vajraḍākinī, Vajrapītā, and Vajramāyā belong to the family of delusion. [And] Vajrajvālā...

Vajralatā, Vajrāveśā, Vajravetālī, Vajrāṅkuśī, and Vajramālā belong to the Ratna family. Vajramālā, Vajralāsyā, Vajrahāsā, Vajrasamcālinī, Vajrapuṣpā, Vajrapadma, and Vajrarāgā belong to [the family of] passion.
O noble ladies, Vajradhātvīśvarī, Vajraspandā, Vajratārā, Vajravilāsinī, Vajramati, Vajrakiṅkiṇī, Vajrakhaṭvāṅgī, and Vajranisvāsā belong to the Samaya family.

"Passion," and so forth. Therein, passion (*rāga*) is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); hatred (*dveṣa*) is the destruction of duality; delusion (*moha*) is the non-cognition of duality. "Samaya" means that which comes from all sides (*samantād eti*) by way of being an emanation (*nirmāṇatayā*). "Sattva" refers to the oneness of the three realms of existence (*tribhava*), because of its utter purity (*suviśuddhatvāt*). "Maṇi" (jewel) is because of its excellence and because of the equality of all Buddhas. These are the six families (*ṣaṭ-kula*). One is the lineage (*gotra*) of the five, while the others are the five lineages of the Bodhisattvas. "Kāma" means a mind accompanied by passion, hatred, and delusion.

Regarding the passage beginning with "attachment" (*rāga*) and so forth: attachment is great compassion; aversion (*dveṣa*) is non-duality; ignorance (*moha*) is non-conceptualization of duality; the so-called "universal commitment" (*samaya*) is universal emanation; the so-called "hero" (*sattva*) is the unification of the three entities, which is the utterly pure realm (*dhātu*); and the "jewel" (*maṇi*) refers to all Buddhas.

This is the excellence of the distinction of equality. By that, there are six families; [or] five families and one. The others are the five families of the bodhisattvas. "Desire" refers to the mind endowed with attachment, aversion, and delusion.
Thus ends the commentary on the third chapter of the *Tattvaviṣadā*, the *Pañjikā* of the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*. O ||
This is the explanation of the third chapter from the *Extensive Commentary on the Reality* (*De kho na nyid rgyas pa*), the *Commentary on the Difficult Points of the Vajrapañjara Ḍākinī*.

"Vajragarbha’s Manifest Enlightenment, the First King of Rituals," and so forth, is easy to understand. "Vajragarbha’s Manifest Enlightenment, the First King of Rituals," and so forth, is easy to understand.

Regarding the body, there is the hand-seal (*karamudrā*). By means of the syllable *HŪṂ*, the vajras, wheels, and so forth are purified for the hands and other limbs. Likewise, from the instruction, there are the seals of the feet, the gaze, and so forth. Regarding the "speech-seal" (*vāṅmudrā*): on the tongue, by means of a white *HŪṂ*, one performs the recitation of the mantra with a white vajra; this is the recitation of the wrathful deity of Cessation (*nirodhakrodha*). Regarding the mind, however, there is the "symbol-seal" (*cihnāmudrā*): having produced it through the mind, one fashions various symbols—such as those cast or engraved—that are appropriate for the respective deities, beginning with the tongs (*saṃdaṃśa*) and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "as for the mudrās of the body," "of the body" refers to the activities of the body. "Mudrā" means that one should not separate [the hands]; it refers to placing the vajra, wheel, and so forth upon the fingers of the hands that have been purified by the *hūṃ*-vajra. Likewise, the mudrās of moving the feet, the gaze, and so forth should also be maintained. As for speech...

"Seal" (*mudrā*) refers to the activity of speech; it is the recitation of mantras such as those of the wrathful deities, characterized by a white vajra born from the syllable *hūṃ*. Regarding the phrase "the seal of the mind is not a sign," the seals for the mental practice consist of dry signs such as the meditative image of the deity’s form and so forth.

"Seal" (*mudrā*) means by way of that which is not to be transgressed. In some readings, it is "the seal of the sign in the painting" (*citre cihnamudrā*). In the painted mandala (*lekhyamaṇḍala*), it is the seal of the sign; however, in the maṇḍala of the assembly (*gaṇamaṇḍala*), because of the observation of variety, the seal of the sign is fashioned from gold and other materials. That very same thing is the "meditation mandala" (*dhyānamaṇḍala*). That same seal of the sign consists of the tongs and so forth, because they are explicitly mentioned. Therefore, for Pukkasī and the others, the Śarabha and so forth should be understood according to the painted mandala. "The tongs in the right hand," and so on, is easy to understand. "Moving through all space" (*sarvākāśacara*): "all space" is the gnosis of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*).

In some [tantric] texts it is stated that "the sign is the mudrā. Here, "sign" (*ri mo*) refers to the mandala made of colored powders; "mudrā" refers to the signs to be drawn there, such as those made of gold and other materials. The phrase "that itself is the meditative concentration mandala" means that it is the sign of the deity of meditative concentration—the sign of the mind—and this is explicitly mentioned as being on a dry surface and so forth.

Thus, one should understand that below those [deities], following the mandala designs of Pukkasī and the others, lions and so forth are to be drawn. "In the right hand, holding a snake" is easy to understand. Regarding the phrase "wandering throughout space," "all space" refers to the primordial wisdom of prajñā.

Regarding the *Ḍākinītantra*: there is the causal tantra (*hetutantra*), the resultant tantra (*phalatantra*), and the method tantra (*upāyatantra*). It is called "causal" because it leads toward or attains the state of the result; thus, the *dharmadhātu*—which has no beginning or end—is so named because it takes all phenomena as its objective support. Because that cause possesses an unassailable result, it is the "result"; the meaning is that there is an absence of discursive conceptualization (*vikalpa*) that could be subsumed [by other causes]. The "method tantra" consists of mantra, mudrā, maṇḍala, and so forth. It is the "supreme" among all tantras because it is the unsurpassed yoga (*yoganiruttara*); it is superior to the *kriyā*, *caryā*, and other [lower] classes.

"Superficial and difficult to fathom. It is superficial because it is dependent upon skillful means (*upāya*). It is difficult to fathom because self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), which is the fruit-dependent [aspect], is not within the sphere of others; for it is of the nature of the self-awareness of the Buddhas. Therefore, it is indeed known, yet it is not known at all. The remainder has not been explained because it is easy to understand.

Regarding what is called "The Tantra of the Ḍākinīs," it consists of the causal tantra (*hetu-tantra*), the resultant tantra (*phala-tantra*), and the method tantra (*upāya-tantra*). In that context, it is the "cause" because it benefits and proceeds toward the nature of the result; it is the intrinsic nature of the basic space (*dhātu*) of all phenomena, which is without beginning or end as an object of observation. Therefore, it is the "result" because there is no gathering of a result apart from the cause. There is no inherent nature of the realization that is to be gathered.

Because of that, the so-called "Tantra of Methods" refers to the mantras, mudrās, maṇḍalas, wheels, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the guru of all tantras," this means it is the Unsurpassed Yoga Tantra (*anuttarayogatantra*), because it serves as the superior authority over the Action (*kriyā*) and Performance (*caryā*) Tantras and so on. As for the phrase "vast and its depth difficult to fathom," "vast" refers to the methods.

"Continuum" (rgyud) refers to the continuum of the fruit, which is difficult to fathom. This is because the wisdom of the five families of Buddhas is not within the sphere of experience of others. Therefore, regarding the statement, "Thus, it is the family and that which is unknown to others," the remainder is easy to understand and has not been explained.

"Abiding in the samādhi of supreme bliss" means as follows: having performed the preparation of the maṇḍala and so forth with various ritual implements according to the instruction, and having entered the maṇḍala by way of the procedure for the disciple's entrance; and having received from the Lord of the Circle (cakrādhipa) everything from the water initiation up to the final authorization (*anujñā*); and immediately after hearing the reality of the truths and so forth; while the eyes and upper garment are bound with a cloth over which the *vighnāri* mantra has been recited; there arises in the heart—the heart of Heruka filled with supreme bliss—a samādhi in which the body is filled with atoms of light rays from the syllable *Aḥ*. That very state is "abiding in the samādhi of supreme bliss."

Regarding the phrase "abiding in the joy of supreme meditative absorption (*samādhi*)," it means that after performing the construction of the maṇḍala with various offering materials according to the oral instructions, one first enters the maṇḍala oneself through the ritual for admitting the disciples. Then, having received the empowerments—beginning with the water empowerment and ending with the subsequent permissions—from the Lord of the Wheel (*cakreśvara*), one proclaims the blessing of truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*).

At the end of the neck, one should wrap a cloth mask and upper garment made from the rags of those who have been devoured by the *bhūta* spirits. At the heart, one abides in the samādhi of the nature of supreme joy, wherein the light rays from the heart of Heruka—emanating from the syllable *HĪ*—fill the entire body down to its subtlest atoms.

Regarding "the consecration of knowledge" (*vidyāseka*): it is called "knowledge" (*vidyā*) because it is the cause for the transformation of ignorance. They are called "consecrations" (*abhiṣeka*) because one is consecrated by means of them. In that regard, for the sake of sentient beings, there are six types of purification for the six obscurations—such as the mental formation of the conceptualization of a self—and these are the six consecrations, respectively.

That which is called "the empowerment of knowledge" (*vidyā-vaśitā*) is the reversal of ignorance; because it cleanses that very [ignorance], it is an empowerment. In this regard, there are six types of empowerments that cleanse, respectively, the obscurations regarding reality (*tattva*), the object (*artha*), sentient beings (*sattva*), the self (*ātman*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and the consciousness of engagement (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
As it is said in this very [text]: "Furthermore, from this very [source]..."
The first is by the sprinkling of water; the second by the crown-consecration;
the third by the vajra-consecration; the fourth is self-sovereignty;
the fifth is by the name-consecration; and the sixth is indeed that of the Perfect Buddha.
The vase initiation is the seventh, while the secret initiation is the eighth;
the ninth is from the wisdom initiation. It is said:

"The water initiation is the first, the crown initiation is the second, the vajra initiation is the third, and the self-lord initiation is the fourth. The name initiation is the fifth, the Buddha initiation is the sixth, the vase initiation is the seventh, the secret initiation is the eighth, and the wisdom-gnosis initiation is the ninth."
Later, they will explain three below: "The three will be explained below. If it is asked, "Well then, how is the first *saṃbuddha* the sixth? [the answer follows].

With respect to the five initiations purified by the five wisdoms, such as the mirror-like wisdom and so forth, the sixth [initiation] would indeed be the first in terms of the sequence; however, because it is the purification of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), it is established as the sixth. If one asks: "If this is the first initiation bestowed by the Perfect Buddha (*saṃyaksambuddha*), how is it designated as the sixth?"—although it is the first in the order of stages, it is established as the sixth in dependence upon the purification of the five wisdoms, beginning with the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). Since it is the purification of the objects of knowledge, it is posited as the sixth.

Immediately after entering there, one should cast a garland into the maṇḍala while reciting: "Accept it, O Vajra-hoḥ! Having caught the white flower-garland that has fallen upon a symbol or near a symbol, one should bind it on the disciple's head while saying: "O you of great strength, accept this! Because it is accepted by the Perfect Buddhas, this is the first, the Flower Empowerment, which is the nature of the purity of the dharmadhātu, without beginning or end.

Following the entry into the maṇḍala, one should cast a flower garland into the maṇḍala while reciting *pratīccha vajra hoḥ*. Whichever deity’s [symbol] the flower falls upon, that is the mantra for that deity; then, while reciting *pratigṛhṇa svamimāṃ sattvāya mahābala*, one binds the flower garland upon the head of the disciple. This is for the purpose of formally accepting [the disciple] as a Buddha.
This is the empowerment of the Perfect Buddha, the Empowerment of the Flower Garland. It is the nature of the utterly pure *dharmatā*, beginningless and endless.

"By the water of one's own vidyā-person, with the eight vases all around"—the Lord of the Mandala is joined with his own *vidyā*. His "water" is that which arises from union (*samāpatti*); it is the water of *bodhicitta*. Alternatively, some say it refers to all [the waters] arising from the union produced by worship. By means of that, the goal to be accomplished should be understood as essentially one.

Regarding the phrase, "The water of the self-knowing person, together with the eight vases from all sides": the so-called "water of the self-knowing person" refers to the vase of victory (*vijaya-kalaśa*), which is filled with the water of bodhicitta arising from the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of the Lord of the Mandala who possesses awareness. Alternatively, it refers to the eight vases that arise from the offerings of meditative absorption.
One should perform the *paribhoga* (enjoyment); together with that, one should cause [the meaning] to be understood as being of a single essence.

Together with the eight vases in all eight directions, there [should be] one in sequence at the door and corners for the goddesses, marked with their respective symbols. Its interior is filled with that *bodhicitta* and marked with the symbol of Vighnāri. Regarding its interior, it is because of the statement: "One should not omit the tenth, the Vighnāri-vase, by implication."

"From all sides" (*kun nas*) means residing in the eight directions; it is marked by the symbols of the eight goddesses who reside at the four gates and the intermediate points, and its interior is likewise filled by them. "Ten" refers to being marked by the symbols of the obstructing spirits and enemies, for it is said that one must not have fewer than ten vases.

"To satisfy" means one should consecrate him. "The Wielder of the Vajra" refers to meditating on Heruka. "By the manifestation of the Vajra-mind" means by the manifestation of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) through the transformation of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Alternatively, "Vajra-minds" refers to the Tathāgatas; by their manifestation. The crown fashioned from those [jewels], such as the variegated ones and so forth—one should give that crown to the disciple. "One should manifest the Vajra-sun" means the disciple, and by the word "and" (*ca*), the crown transformed from that [sun].

"Should be meditated upon" means it should be purified. Upon what? It says, "having visualized the Holder of the Vajra," which refers to the disciple visualized as Heruka. "Having thoroughly visualized [him] as Vajrasattva" refers to the transformation of the state of the ālayavijñāna (all-basis consciousness).

This is the meditation on the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). Alternatively, "Vajrasattva" refers to the Tathāgatas. "Well-meditated upon" means that they have fashioned and marked the crown [of the disciple]. Regarding the phrase "one should well meditate on the Vajra Sun," this refers to the disciple. Through empowerment, from that transformation, he becomes the crest ornament (*uṣṇīṣa*).

Regarding the phrase "by means of the application of the vajra-gāthā": for both empowerments, one should recite *vajrābhiṣiñcet*. Regarding the phrase "the great nine-pronged vajra": it is indeed five-pronged.

Now, one might wonder how there can be a "nine-pronged" [vajra] in that case; thus he says: the four prongs on the lower side have the nature of the female gatekeepers (*dvārapālī*); the four prongs on the upper side have the nature of the goddesses of the corners (*koṇadevī*). By virtue of the purity of the nature of the Lord of the Maṇḍala and his two Vidyās, the single central prong constitutes the nine-pronged [vajra].

Regarding how they are joined: the four corners of the lower surface are the nature of the gatekeepers; the four corners of the upper surface are the nature of the four goddesses of the boundaries; and the two central corners of the upper and lower surfaces are the nature of the Lord of the Mandala and his consort.

And so it was said by Garbhapāda in the *Sarvabuddhasamāyoga-ṭīkā*: "The four corner-spires are the nature of the purification of the four goddesses, Samvarī and the rest; likewise, the others are those of Turaṅgamā and the rest. Thus, the venerable master Ānandagarbha stated in his commentary on the *Buddhasamāyoga*: "It is like the corners of the sides; they are the purification of the goddesses beginning with Prabhāvatī, while the other four are those of Turaṅgamā and the rest."

"The central trident has the nature of Vajrasattva; it may be a five-pronged or a nine-pronged trident. Thus, since the Middle Way is the nature of Vajrasattva and there is no division within the Middle Way, even the number five becomes nine. As it is said in the *Catuḥpīṭha*: "The center is all of Vairocana."
Furthermore, as it is stated in the *Vajracatuṣpīṭha*:

"The central shaft is Vairocana by nature; likewise, its upper and lower natures are to be understood in that same way. Thus, the central [shaft] is the essence of Vairocana, and its two aspects—the upper and the lower—are likewise to be understood as being of that same nature.

The great vajra is the nature of Padmanarteśvara through the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇā*). Having placed it at his heart with his own hand—"having grasped it at the heart," is the ellipsis—[he sees] the disciple in the form of Lokeśvara, that is, in the appearance of Padmanarteśvara. "Now consecrated" means: now by the Buddhas, that is, by all the perfectly enlightened ones (*sarvasambuddha*). "This is that state of all the Buddhas" means: this very thing is the producer of all enlightenment. "The disciple as the best of horses" means: like a supreme steed. "Embraced by the goddess Tārā" means: united in union with Tārā.

"Vajra Great One" (Vajramahā) refers to the nature of Padmanarteśvara, which is the wisdom of individual discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). "In the heart" means that which is to be grasped remains there. "The disciple shall be empowered by the Lord of the World" means that the disciple is to be visualized in the form of Padmanarteśvara. "Today you are being consecrated" means that therein, by the Truly Perfect Buddhas (*samyaksaṃbuddha*), [you are empowered].

Thus, "this is the nature of all Buddhas" means that it generates all forms of enlightenment. "The disciple, the supreme steed goddess" refers to Vajravārāhī. "One should visualize being embraced by Tārā" means entering into union with Tārā.

"By the Lord of Vajras" means the lord of the vajras; he is the one who disciplines [beings] through the form of the perfectly pure accomplishment of activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna*). "Making the sound of the vajra-bell" means that after embracing Tārā with the vajra and the vajra-bell, he makes the sound of the vajra-bell. "Having made the disciple Vairocana" means having produced him in the form of Śāśvata through the purity of the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu*. "Placing his hand on his head by name" should be understood as meaning that he should confer the empowerment by means of the name.

"Vajrapati" means the Lord of Vajras, so called for the sake of training those to be tamed through the purification of the *jñāna* (wisdom) of diligent application (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna*). "With his hand, he rings the vajra-bell" means that, possessing both the vajra and the bell, he embraces Tārā and subsequently rings the bell. Having caused the disciples to appear [as deities], one should generate them in the form of the Permanent One (*nitya-rūpa*), and then [bestow] the name initiation (*nāmābhiṣeka*).

"Bestowal" (*bskur ba*) refers to the conferral of empowerment (*dbang bskur ba*) by placing the hand upon the crown of the disciple's head while assigning a name; it is the nature of the utterly pure *dharmadhātu*.

Regarding the phrase "whatever appears": whatever appears in the form of a water-consecration (*jalābhiṣeka*), that is "the entirety" (*sarvasva*). That alone is "the whole self," meaning it is the primary or principal [empowerment].

Regarding the teaching on the withdrawal of the six faculties, it says "whatever," and so forth. "Whatever appears" refers to appearances such as water and so on. "The universal lord" means that very [consciousness] is the self-nature of all. "Lord" (gtso bo) means the master (bdag po).

Śrī Heruka—this is an illustration by way of oneself; he is to be seen as having the nature of a universal monarch (cakravartin) for each [practitioner]. "Phenomena" (*dharmāḥ*) refers to the qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadharma*); "pure by nature" means they are intrinsically pure (*prakṛti-pariśuddha*). "That which" (*yat*) means because. "The consecration of the pure form" refers to the Buddha-knowledge, which is the state of being a mass [of merit] in the form of the consecration with flowers and so forth belonging to the Buddhas. The particle *hi* has the sense of "indeed. These are the six knowledge-consecrations (*vidyābhiṣeka*).
If only this much is done here, the vow and the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*) are performed at that very moment.

*He ru ka* is an abbreviation; one should regard it as the individual Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*). *Gang* means "for which" or "because of which. *Rang bzhin dag pa* refers to those who have been purified through the ritual ablutions of empowerment. *Dri med* is because they are naturally pure by their very nature. *Chos* refers to the Buddhas.

It is so. If one asks what that reality is, it is called "the wisdom of the Buddha," which consists of the five wisdoms and the sixth, the realm of the utterly pure dharmatā. If one asks whether it is limited to those alone, it is not; it is also to be understood as the ascetic practices and the prophecies.

He says that very thing: "The Vajra of the Accomplishment of All Tathāgatas. The vajra of the accomplishment of all Tathāgatas is perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*). "Abide in the pledge" (*samaye tiṣṭha*): the pledge (*samaya*) is that which has attained this designation of the pledge; abide therein. "I am this" (*eṣo ’ham*): [this] is indeed the Vajra of the Accomplishment of All Tathāgatas. He indicates that very same thing with the six syllables: *hīḥ*. Because it has reached the state of being free from the pursuit of the two causes, *hīḥ* is the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). The four short *hī*s are as follows: *hī*.

The pride of inferiority and superiority passes away through the absence of conceptualizing consciousness (*vikalpavijñāna*). It indicates the knowledge of the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu* by means of the performance of the activity of observing equality. "HŪṂ": the mind (*manas*) is HŪṂ, being empty from beginning to end of the appearance of the grasped object (*grāhya*) and so forth; it expresses the purification of the consciousness of the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu*.

Regarding the passage beginning with "This very [truth] was spoken," *sarvatathāgatasiddhibhadra* means "the perfect enlightenment. *Samayatiṣṭha* means that because one has attained the all-pervading primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), it is the "pledge" (*samaya*), which is the perfect enlightenment; *tiṣṭha* means "abide in that. This very [meaning] is taught by the six syllables, among which *hi* signifies the ultimate meaning.

Because it is free from the dust of the faults of sentient beings, it is the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). "Hi hi hi hi" means being free from the stains of self-grasping and so forth; it is the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*), the wisdom of individual discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), the wisdom of all-accomplishing activity (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), and the wisdom of the thoroughly pure expanse of phenomena (*dharmadhātu-viśuddhi-jñāna*).
"Hūṃ" signifies the purity of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), which is free from the stains of grasping at objects and so forth.

"By means of the ritual procedure for all methods" (*sarvopāyikavidhānena*) refers to the requisites for the mandala. "All methods" (*sarvopāyika*) means everything; their "procedure" (*vidhāna*) is the offering according to the proper rule. The meaning is: by means of the meditative resolve (*adhimokṣa*) that [all things] are like an illusion and so forth. "One should worship all the unsurpassed [deities]" means by means of outer, secret, and essential (*tattva*) offerings. "Vow" (*vrata*) means an unbreakable commitment.
"Supreme offerings of all kinds" refers to the outer, secret, and suchness offerings. "Vow-holder" (brtul zhugs) refers to the indivisible commitment (*samaya*).

Following the recitation of the verse, [the vajra is passed] from the hand of the master to the hand of the disciple. Regarding the phrase "without beginning or end": that which has no beginning or end is the *dharmadhātu*, the *dharmakāya*.

Regarding the phrase "From hand to hand, O Vajra," this refers to the recitation of the verse followed by the master placing [the vajra] from his own hand into the hand of the disciple. If one asks what it is like, it is expressed by the words "without beginning or end" and so forth; "without beginning or end" refers to the Dharmakāya, which is the utterly pure nature of phenomena (dharmatā).

"Being a *sattva*" means having the single flavor (*ekarasa*) of all phenomena. "Vajrasattva" means having the nature of Akṣobhya and being the essence of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*). "Mahārata" means possessing the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) by virtue of the nature of Ratnasaṃbhava. "Samantabhadra" means Amitābha, whose contemplation (*kalpana*) is auspicious (*bhadra*) in every respect, by virtue of the nature of discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). "The Self of All" means Amoghasiddhi in form, being the self of all through the nature of all-accomplishing wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*).

"Vajrasattva" means the single taste of all phenomena (*dharmas*). "Vajrasattva" refers to the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), which is the nature of Akṣobhya. "Mahāsukha" (Great Bliss) refers to the jewel-producing [wisdom] and the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*). "Samantabhadra" means "universally virtuous," and is the nature of Amitābha and the discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*).
The one called "Lord of All" (*sarvādhipati*) is the nature of Amoghasiddhi and the wisdom of the performance of activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*).

Regarding "Lord of Vajragarvā": he is the husband of Vajragarvā, whose essence is the wisdom of the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu* by way of the nature of Vairocana. "Lord" (*pati*) means the sovereign of all Buddhas.
"Vajragarbha" refers to the wisdom of the utterly pure *dharmadhātu* and the mode of Vairocana. "The Principal" (*gtso bo*) means he is the principal among the Tathāgatas.
*iyaṃ setyādi* | *prajñāghoṣānugeti* | It awakens each respective dharma within the mental continuums of all those to be trained; it follows after that [awakening], thus it is "following" (*anuga*).
"Accompanied by Wisdom and Radiance" means that one realizes the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā) in accordance with the individual dispositions of all those to be trained.

"Having taken up all assurances," and so forth—by this verse, it is indicated that Śākyamuni himself [performed this]. "Himself" means by his own self. It should be understood in this way here as well. With the left hand holding the heart, the fist, and the robe, while the right hand displays the gesture of granting boons, standing with feet together, one should receive the prophecy together with all the Tathāgatas.

Regarding the phrase "having expelled all defects into the pit," this refers to the words beginning with "by means of seeing and entering. One should transform oneself into Śākyamuni; that is to say, holding the religious robe at the heart with the left fist and forming the mudrā of supreme generosity with the left hand, one should stand in the even-footed posture (samapada) and receive the prophecy together with the Tathāgatas.

*Oṃ eṣo 'ham*, etc. "Having extracted [me] from the miserable states of existence" means from the miserable states of *bhava*. "For the sake of attaining ultimate *bhava*-perfection" means for the sake of attaining non-abiding *nirvāṇa*. In that context, *bhūḥ* refers to the abyss of the seven netherworlds; *bhuvaḥ* refers to the intermediate space; and *svaḥ* refers to heaven. Having attained the empowerment of knowledge (*vidyābhiṣeka*), the three meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) are to be cultivated. To that end, he teaches the application of the three meditative absorptions: "the teacher of the vajra-meditative absorption. He is the "teacher" (*deśaka*) because he teaches the *Ādiyoga*, the *Maṇḍalarājāgra*, and the *Karmarājāgra*.
"In order to perfectly accomplish the welfare of beings" means for the sake of attaining non-abiding nirvāṇa. *Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*.

The phrase "thus" refers to the three worlds. In order to demonstrate that one who has attained mastery over the vidyās cultivates the three samādhis, the text states "then wisdom," and so forth. The "vajra samādhi" refers to the samādhis of the initial application (*prayoga*), the supreme sovereign of the maṇḍala (*maṇḍalarājāgri*), and the supreme sovereign of activity (*karmarājāgri*).

"Having emanated that which is called the Vajra-samaya": having meditated on one's own seed-syllable upon the sun or moon at one's own heart, having emanated its rays and focused upon the Lord of the Mandala, as well as the Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas, one should utter these words: "The Three Jewels are my refuge... [8! damaged]

Having brought forth the vajra-samaya, one should visualize one’s own seed-syllable upon a moon or sun disk at one’s heart. From that, rays of light are emitted, and having visualized the Cakravartin Guru, the Buddhas, and the Bodhisattvas, one should recite: “I take refuge in the Three Jewels,” and so forth.

And it should be understood as follows: "One should perform the seven purifications. These are: confession of misdeeds, rejoicing in merit, dedication of merit, going for refuge to the Three Jewels, supplication [to the Buddhas], entreaty [for their teaching], and taking recourse in the Path. These are the seven purifications.

The phrase "the Guru Vajradhara" is an elliptical designation. "Offerings" refers to the offerings made by the offering goddesses who have emerged from the light at one's own heart. "Purifying the sevenfold [limbs]" refers to the confession of misdeeds, the rejoicing in merit, the complete dedication of merit, taking refuge in the Three Jewels, making requests, and supplicating for the path.

"Having generated the mind of awakening (bodhicitta)" refers to the ultimate [bodhicitta] and that which is subsequently attained— the protection wheel and so forth, which arise from pure mundane gnosis.

"The visualization of the source of phenomena (dharmodaya) is vast, white, and has the nature of Vajradhara; having meditated there upon the abode of the Buddhas" means that one should meditate on the gabled palace (kūṭāgāra) through the transformation of Vairocana, who arises from the wheel of the syllable *Bhrūṃ* and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) situated upon a double-vajra atop a universal lotus within that [source of phenomena].

Regarding the phrase "meditate on the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) as the abode": having first meditated upon the protective wheel, one meditates thereon the mudrā of the source of phenomena—the nature of the thirteenth stage together with the stage of conduct through aspiration—which is subtle at its base and vast above, white in color, and the very essence of Vajradhara. Within that, one meditates on the Buddha’s palace.
Upon the vajra and lotus, one meditates on the four great elements arising, and from the syllable *Bhrūṃ* and a wheel, Vairocana completely transforms into a tiered palace.

"One should meditate on the fivefold form" means: by means of the fifteen vowels beginning with *a*, one meditates on the moon; by means of the thirty-four consonants beginning with *ka*, the sun. Within the two suns situated upon their respective centers (*varaṭaka*), one meditates on a skull marked with a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) and a curved knife, which have arisen from the transformation of the syllables *hūṃ* and *āṃ* respectively. Having thus meditated on the seed-syllables, this is the wisdom of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).

Regarding the phrase "one should meditate on the five aspects": from the fifteen vowel-syllables beginning with *ā*, there arises the moon; from the thirty-four consonants beginning with *ka*, there arises the sun. By the light of that [sun], all the qualities of the Buddha are summoned and drawn in like stars. These should be viewed as mutually reflecting one another like reflections, which is the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). Above that, [the syllables] *ṣṭum* and *ām*...

From the complete transformation, there arises in sequence a skull marked with various vajras and a curved knife, with the seed-syllable marked upon the sun at their centers; this is the wisdom of individual discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).

Through the radiation of rays from those [seeds], the fifteen goddesses emanate and perform the welfare of the world; thus, it is the wisdom of all-accomplishing action (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*). Having withdrawn [the radiation], one should meditate on the fivefold form consisting of the essence of primordial wisdom (*jñānātmaka*), which results from the transformation of the moon, sun, seed-syllables, and signs—thus it has been explained.

From its light rays, the wheel of the mandala of the fifteen goddesses emanates to perform the benefit of sentient beings; this is the wisdom of all-accomplishing action (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). Then, having condensed [the deities] into the seed syllables, hand symbols, and the moon and sun disks, from the total transformation of all these arises the so-called "Primordial Being," Samantabhadra, with sixteen arms, eight faces, and four legs, possessing the colors described below.
"Endowed with the marks and signs" refers to the extremely pure primordial wisdom (*suviśuddha-jñāna*), which is the fivefold manifest enlightenment;

thus it is said that "one should meditate. Regarding the instruction "one should arrange the *ḍākinī*-wheel," this means the passion for the Vajra. The word "subsequently" (*paścāt*) is to be understood as meaning "at the end. "When the Gandharva has entered, one should recollect the melting descent" means one should recollect the melting descent of the form of the deity about to arise. Having caused [the seed-syllable] to enter through one's own mouth, [one places] *hūṃ* and *aṃ* within the lotus of one's own consort. Both [syllables] are melted by the moon. One should recollect the melting descent like a blazing fire.

Regarding the phrase "the wheel of ḍākinīs emanates," it should be joined to the end of the verse beginning with "Then, the Great Vajra Passion. As for the line "having entered like a gandharva, one falls and the melting is recollected": one should visualize the deity in the form of one being born, [uttering] "Hūṃ Āṃ."

Having inserted [the seed syllables] between two red [syllables], visualize that the four syllables emerge from one’s own mouth and enter the heart of the lotus; contemplate that great passion melts, and through the power of its light, meditate that even the primordial being, together with his awareness, becomes blazing with light and takes on a form of molten radiance like a flickering flame.

"He is exhorted by the goddesses of the corners" means that he is exhorted by the four Ḍākinīs who originate from the melting [of passion], with songs beginning with "O Vajradoṣa. "The leader of the wheel is exhorted" refers to his being exhorted through the entry of the four goddesses and the withdrawal of the melting [fluid].

Regarding the phrase "the goddesses of the six directions should be exhorted," this means that the four ḍākinīs arising from the light of the request should take up the song beginning with "O you who are named Hatred-Vajra" and so forth. The phrase "having exhorted the Guide of the Wheel" means that after being exhorted by song, the four goddesses dissolve back into the form of the request; through the complete transformation of the seed-syllables and signs, [the faces and other features arise].
She sits in a posture with a body possessing the [mudrās] that arise from below.

*Vajrak* | In the nose is Mātsaryavajrā; in the mouth is Rāgavajrā; in the body is Īrṣyāvajrā; and in the mind is Nairātmyaḍākinī. Their colors and so forth will be explained later. Regarding the phrase "one should place the three vajras": one should place the three vajras at the heart, throat, and crown—namely, Khecarī, Bhūcarī, and Pātālavāsinī.

Regarding the phrase "ignorance and so forth in the eyes and so forth": for the eyes, there is Ignorance-Vajrī; for the ears, Hatred-Vajrī; for the nose, Greed-Vajrī; for the tongue, Attachment-Vajrī; for the body, Jealousy-Vajrī; and for the mind, there is Nairātmyā-Ḍākinī. Their colors and other attributes will be explained below. These three vajras reside in the three places.

Regarding the term *dgod* (to arrange): one arranges the three types of goddesses—the Sky-Wanderers (*khāspyod ma*), Earth-Wanderers (*sa spyod ma*), and Subterranean-Wanderers (*sa 'og na spyod pa*)—at the locations of the heart, the throat, and the crown.

In the moon at each respective heart, there are the three syllables *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*. Impelled by the rays from the seed-syllable *kṛ*, the eight goddesses hold vases in their lotus hands; this is the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), which is the specific distinction.

On that day, one should visualize the syllables *hūṃ*, *āḥ*, or *oṃ* in the moon at the heart as being blue, red, and white in color, respectively. Following that, in order to demonstrate the conferral of empowerment by requesting it, it is said: "The empowerment shall be conferred by the eight consorts. From the seed-syllables of the skull-cup and the *vīṇā* (lute) situated upon a sun disk at one's own heart, [the consorts arise].

One should visualize that one is being consecrated on the crown of the head by goddesses of the lineage, who hold lotuses adorned with vases filled with nectar, urged by the light of *Bai-’od* (Vairocana).

Regarding the phrase "the vajra-affection (*vajrānurāgaṇa*) afterwards": the *vajras* are the Tathāgatas; their affection (*anurāgaṇa*) occurs after the purification of the lotus and the vajra, having caused all the Tathāgatas to enter [the disciple]. *Oṃ sarvatathāgatānurāgaṇavajrasvabhāva...* [8! damaged]...

Regarding the phrase "then, [he] is attached to the vajra": the *vajras* are the Tathāgatas. Their subsequent attachment consists of joining the vajra and the lotus, and through the illusory words of their union, all the Tathāgatas enter into oneself with the mantra: *oṃ sarvatathāgatānurāgaṇavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*. By means of this, one enjoys great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

One should place [the deities] in the corners. Regarding "the entry into the form of gnosis" (*jñānākārapraveśana*) once again: it should be understood that, having summoned the mandala of gnosis by means of the rays from the seed-syllable of the heart, one performs the expulsion of obstacles and worship, and then, having drawn it in, caused it to enter, and bound it, one brings it under control.

This very day is the first meditative absorption (*prathama-samādhi*) consisting of the nature of the *svābhāvika-kāya*. Then, from the complete transformation of their respective seed-syllables within a lotus, as each of those syllables is recited, the goddesses of the gates and the intermediate directions are to be emanated and projected to their respective locations. "The wisdom-wheel (*jñāna-cakra*) is to be inserted" means that by the light arising from those seed-syllables, the wheel of wisdom...
Having summoned [the deity], one again performs purification, makes offerings, and accomplishes the rites of summoning, causing entry, binding, and bringing under control.

"Furthermore, the tasting of nectar (*amṛtāsvādana*)" should be understood as occurring after the praise. "And the worship with the eight goddesses" refers to the procedure beginning with the visualization of the seed-syllable in one's own heart, [the offering of] water for the feet, and so forth; this is the tasting of nectar. "Then one should meditate upon the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*)" means that because the state of equality with the Lord of the Six Chakras is indicated by the six syllables, it is the six-limbed [practice]. Regarding that: "Black, red, then yellow, green, blue, and white, in sequence"—one should meditate on the wheel together with its leader as consisting of nothing but innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), since this has been stated. Its nature is that of the Enjoyment Body (*sāṃbhogikakāya*).

Regarding the phrase "then one should taste the nectar," it should be connected with the words "one should praise the Lord of the Mandala" which follow. "Having worshipped by the eight goddesses" refers to the worship performed by the eight vidyās emanated from the seed-syllable at one's own heart. "One should praise the Lord of the Mandala" means:

"To be combined with the song arising from the *og nas* [the lower part]": this means that one should meditate on the six limbs as being the nature of the six Universal Monarchs (*cakravartin*) of the six colors. In that regard, one should meditate on the lords of the wheels as having the nature of the simultaneously arisen joy (*sahaja-ananda*), following the sequence of black, red, yellow, green, blue, and white.

*Bya'o*. These are the supreme king of mandalas, the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) whose nature is the Body of Perfect Enjoyment (*saṃbhogakāya*); this is the second [stage]. [The third stage is] the application to one's own respective gnosis; by this is meant the meditative absorption named "the Supreme King of Action," whose nature is the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Regarding the phrase "empowered by the empowerment of the self" (*bdag byin brlabs pas byin gyis brlab*): the "empowerment of the self" is one's own primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), and "empowering others" by means of that is the application [of it] as their own primordial wisdom. From the nature of the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of these, there is the third meditative absorption (*samādhi*) called "Supreme King."

The summarized meaning should be understood as being applicable to our own proof. According to the system of the Tantra, one's own self-consecration and the consecration by that [deity], as well as the vision of the five signs, will be explained in the fourteenth chapter.

Whatever that may be, it should be understood as a *sādhana*. First, what arises from the system of the tantras shall be applied here: the self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) is taught in the fourteenth chapter as displaying five types of signs.
Having performed the self-consecration, [one performs] the consecration...
To summarize briefly, I shall now explain:
at the center of the heart is the moon,
and within the form of that moon is the indestructible [syllable].
Light rays of various colors radiate in all directions;
by means of that, one should meditate on Nairātmyā as Vajrī, awakened by the thought of enlightenment.
The yoginī Vajra-nairātmyā visualizes a mustard seed situated within the nose of the ḍākinī; having been exhorted by the ritual dance, she [acts].
Within the inner abode of the nose-tip of the ḍākinī,
one should clearly visualize that which is called "the mustard seed" (yungs kar);
for within a single mustard seed resides the entire world of the three realms, with all its moving and unmoving beings.
For one who meditates in this way, self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) is accomplished.
Thus, the three realms, both moving and non-moving, the entire world without exception— this is what should be meditated upon there.
It is said: "By meditating in this way constantly, the accomplishment of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*) will be attained."

In that regard, "in brief" refers to the sequence. "Situated in the center of the heart" means [the syllable] *ra*. "Pervaded by various rays" means it is endowed with five rays. "By that" means by the seed-syllable *hūṃ*. "One should visualize a vajra" means a blue vajra the size of a barley grain. "One should visualize the Ḍākinī Nairātmyā by means of the vajra" means she is marked by the vajra. "Impelled by awakening" means it falls within the interior of both apertures.

"Condensed" (*mdor bsdus*) means according to the sequence [of the stages]. "In the center of the heart" means within the lotus of wisdom (*prajñā*). "Moon" refers to the moon-maṇḍala. "Indestructible" (*mi shigs pa*) refers to the *bindu*, the crescent moon, and the syllable *hūṃ* adorned with the sixth vowel. "Radiating various rays of light" means possessing the five-colored rays of light. That...

"Visualize the vajra" means that one should visualize a blue vajra, the size of a barley grain, arising from the complete transformation of the syllable *hūṃ*. "Having visualized the Vajra-Nairātmyā Ḍākinī" means [visualizing her] as being marked by the vajra. "Having exhorted with ritual gestures" means causing [her] to descend through the union of the two organs.

Or alternatively, "the moon situated in the center of the heart" refers to the very moon residing in one's own heart. Its meaning as the *anāhata* (unstruck) has been explained previously. [The practitioner visualizes] Nairātmya-Ḍākinī as a minute drop, subtle like a mustard seed, transformed from a vajra. She is so called because she specifically indicates the reality of selflessness (*nairātmyatattva*). Regarding "impelled by awakening": having brought her down from the heart, she is positioned within the nose of the Ḍākinī. The rest is as before.

"Abiding at the tip of the ḍākinī’s nose" means at the boundary of the tips of both nostrils. "The three realms, moving and non-moving" refers to the maṇḍala of the support and the supported. "Therein" means within the vajra-vision. Alternatively, "at the center of the heart" means in one's own heart. The moon and the indestructible have already been explained. "Subtle" means...

"Action" (*kṛtya*) refers to the drop (*bindu*) that is the complete transformation of the vajra. "Nairātmyā Ḍākinī" indicates Nairātmyā herself. "Having exhorted the assembly" means, as previously explained, having exhorted [the deities] residing in the heart. Where? It says, "residing at the tip of the ḍākinīs' noses," which means at the tip of the lotus-nose. The remainder should be applied as previously explained. Subsequently, others were summoned.

Regarding the statement, "Then, by means of the sequence of the ritual, one should perceive the signs," the "sequence of the ritual" refers to the excellence of familiarity (*abhyāsa*). "Gradually" (*krama*) means that the signs arise in succession. Others, however, say that the characteristics of the stages are distinct and that they arise simultaneously.
"First, the form of a cloud" refers to the subtle shimmering rays as fine as mustard seeds. Because it has the appearance of a single mass, it is the "form of a cloud" of Hevajra.
"First, the form of a cloud" means that the first subtle ray of light is as dense as a cloud; this is the milk of Heruka.
"The second is like smoke" means that the second ray of light appears like smoke lingering in the sky; this is the milk of Śāśvata.

"The third is like a firefly" means that "in the sky," which is the *dharmadhātu*, "lights" (*dyotāḥ*) arise; the meaning is that they resemble the form of a Buddha. [The Tibetan text: "The third is like a firefly"; "sky" refers to the *dharmadhātu*. "Arising" (*udaya*) means appearing or being born. It is the light that appears as the body of a Buddha; this is the third, namely, the sun.
"((Nauka))" means having the form of the sky.

Regarding the phrase "blazing like a lamp in the fourth," this refers to the lotus, which blazes like the tip of a lamp flame. Regarding the fifth, "the constant radiance is like a cloudless sky," this refers to the supreme horse (*aśvarāja*), whose radiance appears continuously and clearly, like the aspect of the sky.

"Caused by omniscience" means through the attainment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). "Subsequently, having the form of an illusion" means that once [the mind] has become stable, there is the appearance of the form of an illusion through the radiation and reabsorption of the maṇḍala of the symbols of the five families. "Having the form of an illusion" means having the form of a dream; the meaning is that it becomes manifest through the penetration of reality.

"The cause of omniscience" refers to the attainment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). "Subsequently, in the manner of an illusion" means that, having attained meditative concentration, one dissolves [the visualization] into the mandala of signs; by way of its very falsity, like a dream, one should dissolve it into selflessness (*nairātmya*) in the form of extremely subtle sun and moon mandalas. By this, all duality is empty.

Abiding through the realization of suchness itself—that is, through the opening [of the eyes], meaning the attainment of the reality not yet attained—is the blessing of the stage of practice through aspiration (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*). By means of the manifestation of the all-pervading *dharmadhātu*, through the realization of the equality of self and others, and by virtue of having a body whose nature is the reflection of the infinite wheel of the three truths within the world-realms, one is established upon the *pramuditā* (Joyful) stage.

What is called "momentary transformation" refers to the mind being intensely joyful because it realizes the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) that was previously unrealized. Furthermore, by realizing the meaning of the all-pervading *dharmadhātu*, one perceives the three wheels of oneself and others as equal, appearing as bodies in the manner of reflections; this is the blessing of the stage of Perfect Joy (*pramuditā*).

"In this [state], all stains of affliction (*kleśamala*) have departed without remainder; thus it is *niḥśeṣa* (without remainder). In this [state], the remaining signs such as the immovable (*acala*) and so forth have emerged; thus it is *niḥśeṣa*. The three realms consist of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). "Moving" refers to sentient beings (*sattva*); "non-moving" refers to the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*). That which exists within these is "moving and non-moving. It is accomplished (*sidhyate*), that is, it is brought to completion. *Ā-*"

Regarding the phrase "the three realms, moving and non-moving": "moving" refers to sentient beings, and "non-moving" refers to the vessel-like world (the physical environment). "Without exception" means the entirety of the desire realm and the formless realm. "Accomplished" means attaining the *dharmakāya*, which arises from the complete transformation of the three bases.

"Of the manifestation of gnosis (*jñānavyañjana*)," it is said. This means: of that which has the nature of the mirror-like and other gnoses by way of the *sāmbhogika*-body, whose body is adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*) and the eighty secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*).

"One who possesses a vajra body" refers to entering into the unmoving earth and so forth. What is that? It is stated above as "the body of the *tāla* [palm-tree] trunk," which is the aggregate of gnosis (*jñāna-skandha*), and so on. In this context, the "aggregate of gnosis" is the *saṃbhogakāya* adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs, because it is of the nature of the mirror-like gnosis and the other [four gnoses].

"Of the wise" means that because of his scholarship (*paṇḍitatva*), he brings about the manifestation of the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) through pure worldly conceptualization. "Born from a source" refers to those born from a womb, from an egg, from moisture, or by spontaneous generation. "Attendants" refers to those who have become the retinue of gods, asuras, and humans who have attained excellence; one should cause them all to enjoy [it] through the enjoyment of the unsurpassed Dharma.

"Endowed with intelligence" (*blo ldan*) refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), because it accords with the minds of all wandering beings. It means "wise" (*mkhas pa*) in the sense of knowing all aspects exactly as they are through authentic worldly gnosis (*samyag-lokajñāna*). "The path of the three realms" refers to the nature of the completely pure Buddha-field, which is like a tiered palace. "Luminous" (*gsal ba*)...

"Bā" is because it is fashioned from the seven extremely blazing precious substances. "As long as those born from birth and karma exist" refers to beings comprised by the four modes of birth: those born from a womb, those born from an egg, those born from heat and moisture, and those born spontaneously. "Following after Mahāmudrā" refers to the retinue of distinguished beings, such as deities and others, who have attained Mahāmudrā.
"Having become non-dual, they enjoy all of those" means that they partake in the unsurpassed enjoyment of the Dharma (*anuttara-dharma-bhoga*).

"Eight-faced" (*aṣṭāsya*) is to be taken literally, as it refers to the complete purity of the eight gates of liberation (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa-mukha*). "Possessing light equal to Indra" refers to the color of saffron (*kuṅkuma-varṇa*), because he possesses a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*). "Four-legged" (*caturbhuja*) refers to the complete purity of the four Māras.

"Khaṃ" refers to the black [face], which is purified by the absence of aspiration (*apraṇihita*). "Adorned with white and red" means that the right [face] is white through purification by emptiness (*śūnya*), and the left is red due to passion (*rāga*) through the signless (*animitta*). "Trampled upon by the four Māras" refers to the Māras of the aggregates (*skandha*), afflictions (*kleśa*), death (*mṛtyu*), and the son of a god (*devaputra*).

"His first face is black" means that it is pure through the gateway of signlessness (*animitta*). "Adorned with white and red" means that it is white because the gateway of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) has been purified, and it is red because the gateway of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) is free from attachment. "The four māras are suppressed" refers to the māras of the aggregates (*skandha*), the afflictions (*kleśa*), death (*mṛtyu*), and the son of the gods (*devaputra*).
"Vajradhara upon the crown" refers to Akṣobhya.

The one called the Vajradhara of the Universal Assembly is Akṣobhya. Regarding the phrase "the consorts with various forms": the Vajra of Ignorance is white; the Vajra of Hatred is blue; the Vajra of Avarice is yellow; the Vajra of Attachment is red; and the Vajra of Envy is green.

—Nīlā is united with selflessness (*nairātmya*). "With a skull and a flaying knife in her hands" means she holds a flaying knife in her right hand and a skull-cup in her left. "Standing above the lifeless one" means she stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture upon the sun on the chest of the enemy. Thus, Khecarī and the others have the radiance of their respective seats (*pīṭha*). Regarding Bhūcarī: she is red in color and located at the throat. Regarding Khecarī: [the text is damaged here], as stated by the word... The remainder is easily understood.

Regarding the phrase "The Black Yoginī Nairātmyā holds a curved knife and a skull-cup in her hands": the curved knife is in the right hand and the skull-cup is in the left. Regarding the phrase "She dwells upon a lifeless corpse": she dwells with her left leg extended upon the sun at the heart of a corpse.

"Khecarī" (Sky-Walker) refers to the blue-colored [deity] at the heart; "Bhūcarī" (Earth-Walker) refers to the throat, which is red in color; and "Pātālacarī" (Underworld-Walker) refers to the crown of the head, which is white in color. In this tantra, because they possess the sun's light as their seat, one should meditate upon them within the solar mandala. It is stated that their forms are white. The remainder is easy to understand.

"The vessel of bodhicitta, Meru, the fire-pit, and the great banner" are the symbols of the goddesses of the corners of the dissolution maṇḍala. These correspond respectively to the root gate-guardians; alternatively, one may meditate on them as mere symbols.

"The Vase of Bodhicitta is the great victory banner in the fire-pit" refers to the symbols of the goddesses residing at the boundaries of the condensed maṇḍala. As for those guardians of the gates, they are in their respective order. Alternatively, one may meditate on the symbols alone.
"The means for the gathering [of the deities] should be known as that of the five cakras"; the *sādhana* of the five Cakravartins should be understood from the *Abhyudaya-saṃkṣepa*.
Holding a copper knife, a lotus, and a khaṭvāṅga,
the Nairātmyā bowed;
her sādhana is as follows:
One should write it according to the sequence:
"With the mantra beginning with *rakṣa*, by means of the protection of the place, the yoga, and oneself."

Having first generated the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) through the cultivation of loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables], the mantra practitioner—who knows the procedure for the ten principles and abides in the vow of the commitments (samaya)—should adorn himself with virtues such as renunciation and possess conviction in the profound method. Having smeared the site of the maṇḍala of the glorious *Yoginīvajrapañjara*, he should sit in the vajra-posture upon a soft seat of grass and the like, his sprout-like hands restrained by the mudrā of meditative concentration. Having placed the syllable *Aṃ* upon the sun at his own heart and performed the cleansing of his face and so forth, he should perform the protection of the place, himself, and the yoga with the mantra: *Oṃ rakṣa 2 hūṃ 2 phaṭ*.

One who possesses qualities such as mastery over the thousand mantras and so forth, whose mind is oriented toward enlightenment preceded by loving-kindness and the like, who has been empowered and granted profound authorization within the mandala of the glorious Ḍākinī Vajrajāla, who has deep faith in that very [practice], knows the ten realities, abides by the pledges and vows, and strives to bring his own mantra to fruition.

In some pleasant locations such as mountain passes, snow mountains, and so forth, having smeared a square meditation hut with fragrant substances like sandalwood, one sits upon a comfortable seat in the vajra posture. Forming the leaf-hand gesture (*pallavamuṣṭi*) as the samādhi-mudrā, one visualizes the syllable *Āḥ* upon a sun disk at one’s own heart. Then, having performed acts such as washing the face, [one recites]: *Oṃ rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ*.

Having performed the protection of the site and oneself with the mantra *PHĀṬ PHĀṬ PHĀṬ*, one should visualize the maṇḍala circle before oneself by means of the light from the seed-syllable at one’s own heart.
