Then, having prostrated, one should make offerings as follows: Caurī holds a vessel of the sun; Vettālī has water in her hand; Ghasmarī holds medicine;
Pukkasī holds a vajra in her hand; Śavarī likewise holds nectar; Caṇḍālī plays the hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*); and Ḍombī, embracing [the deity], acts like a man.

Having made offerings with Devarī holding a vessel of jewels, Cakrī holding a vessel of the sun, Vetālī holding a vessel of water, Ghasmarī holding a vessel of medicine, Pukkasī holding a vessel of vajra, and Śavarī holding a vessel of flavors, one should then delight them by having Caṇḍālī beat a small drum and Ḍombī embrace her by the neck.

Thereafter, [recite] "The Three Jewels are my refuge," and so forth: "May I become a Buddha—[attaining] prosperity—for the sake of the beings born within the three realms of existence. Having rejoiced with faith, may I dedicate all merit toward the state of a Victor, free from all conceptual constructions. I go for refuge to the Perfect Buddhas until the limit of the seat of enlightenment; likewise, I go for refuge to the entire Dharma of the Mahāyāna. I go for refuge to the Saṃgha—"

Following that, recite from "I take refuge in the Three Jewels" up to "may I attain Buddhahood for the sake of benefiting migratory beings. Then, say: "In the presence of the assembly of Sugatas, I confess my heaps of misdeeds," and [contemplate] the mass of merit of the Sugata Munis and the sublime beings of the three realms.

"I shall rejoice in the glory of Kyi. And: "Until I reach the heart of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), I take refuge in the Victorious Buddhas who have completely overcome conceptualization. And: "Likewise, I take refuge in the supreme Dharma of the Mahāyāna. And likewise: "In the assembly of non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas..."
Having said, "I go for refuge to the Three Jewels," and "I shall rely upon the unsurpassed path to enlightenment, the King of the Reality of the Vajra Net of Ḍākinīs," one should think:

"That which is conceptualized by discursive movement is not perceived; through the application of non-arising, this arising is proclaimed. Thus, taking as one's object the world—which is like the cloudless midday sky of autumn, free from appearance and free from conceptual proliferation—one should abide [in the thought]: *Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness*.

By means of the yoga of non-arising, according to the principle expressed in the words, "This very arising is proclaimed as [non-arising]," when all phenomena are analyzed, they are not perceived; being without appearance like the center of an autumn sky, one meditates on them as being utterly free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). Then, one performs the consecration by reciting: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*.

With the letter *ra* [one visualizes] the sun, and with the letter *pu*, a ten-spoked wheel, yellow in color, revolving yet appearing as if motionless. Through the yoga of the ten *hūṃ* syllables, one should meditate upon the ten wrathful deities. Thus it is said.

Then, in front [of oneself], from the syllable *raṃ* arises a sun mandala; upon that sun, one should visualize a *hūṃ* from which a vajra emerges. One should meditate on that very vajra as being thoroughly bound by a most excellent lattice. Having thus performed these and other preliminary rites, in its center, from the syllable *bhrūṃ*, there appears a golden ten-spoked wheel, revolving like Mount Meru. Through the union of the ten *hūṃ*s, the ten wrathful deities [arise].

"NI RNAM PAR BSGOM" (Visualize [the syllable] NI): by this, one visualizes the ten wrathful deities (*krodha*). Therein, at the eastern gate is Yamāntaka, blue; at the south is Prajñāntaka, white; at the west is Padmāntaka, red; and at the north is Vighnāntaka, blue. They hold, respectively, a mallet, a staff, a lotus, and a gaping vajra; they are short in stature and adorned with the eight classes of *nāgas*. Their hair is brownish-yellow and stands upright, and their eyes are round and red. They wear crowns of Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Amitābha, and Akṣobhya, and are clothed in tiger-skin garments.

Regarding the manner of [the deities] beginning with La-shar (East) and so forth: Yamāntaka is blue; in the southern direction is Prajñāntaka, white; in the western direction is Padmāntaka, red; and in the northern direction is Vighnāntaka, blue. Respective[ly], they hold a skull-cup, a staff, a lotus, and a raised vajra; they are short in stature with protruding bellies, and are adorned with the eight serpents.

He has matted hair of a brownish-yellow color tied upward; his eyes are red and round. He is adorned with the crown ornaments of Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi, and wears a lower garment of tiger skin.

The corner-krodhas are Mahākṛṣṇa and Śumbha; they hold, respectively, a goad, a staff, a trident, a sword, and a mace. Among them, in the southeast is Ṭakki, adorned with divine ornaments and garments such as excellent jewels. In the southwest is Nīla, holding a blue staff. In the northwest is Mahābala. These two are deformed like Yamāri and the others.

The wrathful deity of the southeast (*āgneya*) is black. From the *hṛdaya* (chest) up to the *uṣṇīṣa* (cranial protuberance), he is adorned with a *uṣṇīṣa*, and he holds a hook, a staff, a trident, a sword, and a pestle. At the boundary of his fire, he is adorned with precious jewels and wears divine garments. In the southwest (*nairṛtya*) is a blue staff. In the northwest (*vāyavya*)...
They are very powerful; they are like Yamāntaka and the others.

In the northeast is Acala, like Ṭakki. Above is Uṣṇīṣa, yellow; below is Śumbha, black. Their ornaments and so forth are like those of Ṭakki. All of these stand upon a sun disc on a double lotus with their feet in the *pratyālīḍha* posture; with their left hands they hold a snake-noose and a raised index finger (*tarjanī*). They are radiant with Akṣobhya-jewels in their crowns. In the center of the five maṇḍalas is one [deity]; or else there are other wrathful deities and so forth.

In the northeast is Acala, who resembles Takki. Above his head is a yellow *uṣṇīṣa*, and below is a black *ūrṇā*. His ornaments and so forth are like those of Takki. All [the deities] stand with their left legs extended upon seats of various lotuses and suns. Their left hands hold a snake-lasso and display the threatening gesture (*tarjanī-mudrā*).
They wear Akṣobhya as their jewel crest-ornament. In the center, there are other wrathful deities within five maṇḍalas.

Then, having determined the three flames, the directional mandalas, and so forth, one should visualize the mudrā called Dharmodayā, which is triangular, resembling the interior of space, white, and situated in the center of a universal lotus and vajra. Within it are the mandalas of wind, fire, water, and earth, corresponding respectively to the syllables Yaṃ, Raṃ, Vaṃ, and Laṃ, and appearing smoke-colored, red, white, and yellow.

Then, having performed the *padmabandha* and other mudrās of the blazing assembly, in the center thereof is the three-cornered mudrā called *dharmodaya*, which has the nature of space. Upon a variegated vajra and lotus, from the seed-syllables *yāṃ*, *rāṃ*, *bāṃ*, and *lāṃ*, there arise the mandalas of wind, fire, water, and the great earth, colored dark blue, red, white, and yellow, respectively.

Therein, a peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) is produced from the transformation of the four great elements, which have been melted by streams of water emerging from the pores of Vairocana—who himself is the transformation of the *bhrūṃ* syllable and its wheel. It is adorned with four gates and four archways (*toraṇa*), joined with four altars (*vedī*), and decorated with silk bands and flower garlands. It contains the seats for the fifteen deities, presided over by the sun upon the heart of a corpse on a universal-petal lotus. Possessing the ego-identification (*ahaṃkāra*): "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra-abode of all Tathāgatas."

From the hair-pores of Vairocana, who arose from the *bhrūṃ* and the wheel, streams of nectar flow down, causing the four elements to melt. From this, a celestial palace is formed, possessing four doors and four porticos, adorned with four horse-ridges and decorated with garlands of flowers. Within it, at the seats of the fifteen deities upon various lotuses and corpse-thrones, there is a sun disk at the heart.
One should meditate on [the deity] adorned with the mandala and recite: *oṃ ārya-tathāgatadhātulya-vajra-svabhāv-ātmako ’ham*.

In that regard, the moon is formed by the fifteen vowels; the sun by the consonants beginning with *ka*; and it becomes expanded through the entry of all the qualities of the Buddhas, like the form of a star.

Then, upon the central seat, one visualizes a moon arising from the fifteen vowels and a sun arising from the thirty-four consonants, such as *ka* and *li*. Through their light, the qualities of the Buddha’s greatness are gathered and expanded accordingly.

And there, having meditated upon that very seed-syllable within the sun of the central *varaṭaka* as transformed by its own vowel and *anusvāra*, one should visualize oneself in the form of Nairātmyā through the process of the emanation and reabsorption of the fifteen Yoginīs from the mouths of its rays.

Above that, the first vowel together with a bindu becomes the seed-syllable itself, which marks a copper knife; through the sequence of emanating and reabsorbing the wheel of the fifteen yoginīs at its light-rays at the gateway, one should meditate on oneself as Nairātmyā.

Having visualized [the deity] as standing in the *ardhaparyaṅka* dance posture upon the sun-disk taken from the departed breath, with a body whose lines are massed together like a dense circle of clouds at the time of universal dissolution, with blazing tawny hair standing erect, incomparable and fashioned from the atoms of the best of sages, with three eyes and red glances, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns, having destroyed the Māras, with a chest adorned by a garland of fifty severed heads, and embellished with the five mudrās; and having contemplated the state of the *dharmadhātu*, which is neither established in existence nor in cessation, one should possess the ego-identity (*ahaṃkāra*) thinking: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*."

He dances with a posture of half-crouching upon the sun above his heart; he wears upward-flaming orange-yellow hair that blazes like the fire at the end of an eon toward the direction of his head; his red, rounded body is composed of the finest atoms of the Supreme Victor, and his three eyes, wide open like the rising sun, incinerate the māras with their radiance; [he is adorned] with a garland of fifty fresh human heads.

If one contemplates [the self] as having the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, which is adorned in the direction of the south, sealed with the five mudrās, and does not abide in either cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) or peace (*śānti*), one should cultivate the pride [of identity] by reciting: *oṃ dharmadhātu svabhāvātmako ’ham*.

Having visualized Nairātmyā, who holds a threatening *kartī* in her right arm, and in her left arm holds a *khaṭvāṅga* by way of a *yajñopavīta* consisting of a vajra and a skull-cup filled with the blood of gods and asuras—one should contemplate that Mohavajrī is in her two eyes; Dveṣavajrikā is in the two ears; Mātsaryakī is said to be in the nose; Rāgavajrikā is in the mouth; Īrṣyāvajrī is in the body; and the Yoginī Nairātmyā is in the mind. Mohavajrā is in the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); Gaurī is in the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā*) and pride (*māna*).
In perception and passion is Ārī; in mental formations and envy is Vajraḍākī; and in the aggregate of consciousness and hatred is Nairātmyā.

With his right hand brandishing a copper knife, and his left hand holding a skull-cup filled with the blood of gods, asuras, and others, as well as a *khaṭvāṅga*, in the manner of making an offering; in his two eyes is Mohavajrī; in his ears is Dveṣavajrī; in his nose is Piśunavajrī; in his tongue is Rāgavajrī; and in his body is Īrṣyāvajrī.

MA'O: the yoginī of selflessness regarding the mind; furthermore, Vajrā regarding the aggregate of form and delusion; Vajragaurī regarding sensation and pride; Pāṇḍarā regarding perception and attachment; Vajradākinī regarding mental formations and envy; and Nairātmyā regarding consciousness and hatred.

Likewise, one should resolve that in the earth element there is Pukkasī in loving-kindness (maitrī); in the water element, Śavarī in compassion (karuṇā); in the fire element, Caṇḍālī in sympathetic joy (muditā); and in the air element, Ḍombī in equanimity (upekṣā). These very goddesses are, respectively, Bhūcarī and Khecarī in relation to visible form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena (dharma). Thus one should cultivate conviction.

Likewise, the earth element and loving-kindness are Pukkasi; similarly, water and compassion are Śāvari; fire and joy are Caṇḍālī; wind and equanimity are Ḍombinī. Through these, one purifies, respectively, internal forms, sounds, smells, and tastes; as for the tactile element and the mental-object element, one should visualize them as Pātālavāsinī and Khecarī.

By means of the syllable *hūṃ* on the moon at the heart, one becomes Khecarī; by means of the syllable *rakta-āḥ* on the moon at the throat, one becomes Bhūcarī; and by means of the syllable *oṃ* on the moon at the head, one becomes Pātālavāsinī. Having thus assumed the ego-identity (*ahaṃkāra*) with the mantras: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the Vajra of all Tathāgatas Khecarī"; "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the Vajra of all Tathāgatas Bhūcarī"; and "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the Vajra of all Tathāgatas Pātālavāsinī."

Having meditated further upon this, one should generate the blue Khecarī from the syllable *hūṃ* on the moon at the heart; the red Bhūcarī from the syllable *āḥ* on the moon at the throat; and the white Pātālī dwelling in the subterranean realm from the syllable *oṃ* on the moon at the head. Then: *oṃ sarvatathāgatakhecari vajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*, *oṃ sarvatathāgatabhūcari vajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*, *oṃ*.
Having generated the pride [of identity] by reciting: *sarvatathāgatavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*, one [visualizes]:

"By means of the rays of light from the syllable *aṃ* on the sun at the hub of the sword upon the sun in the heart, the Tathāgatas are summoned, and one supplicates them, saying: 'May all the Tathāgatas confer empowerment upon me! Then, after a rain of flowers and the sound of drums by those who have assumed the form of Heruka, Locanā and the others sing praises, while Vajrarūpā and the others offer hymns of praise; thus, one is empowered.

From the letter *Āṃ* at the hub of the copper knife within the sun at one’s own heart, light rays emanate and summon the Tathāgatas. With the words, “May all the Tathāgatas bestow empowerment upon me,” they transform into the form of Heruka. Accompanied by a rain of vajras and the sound of drums, Locanā and the others sing songs of praise, while Vajrarūpī and the others offer hymns of praise and worship, and then confer the empowerment.

As she is being consecrated, Akṣobhya shall become the Jina upon her head. Possessing the pride [of identity] with the thought: *Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra-consecration of all Tathāgatas*, this is the meditative absorption (samādhi) called "Initial Yoga" (*ādiyoga*), and it is the Svābhāvikakāya.
This is the first meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of the application to the nature of the *svabhāvakāya*.

From the seed-syllable at one’s own heart, one should emanate fourteen lunar and solar disks and place them upon the suns at the hearts of fourteen corpses. As before, one should visualize [the deities] as being produced from the seed-syllables of the *kartti* (knife), the *varaṭaka* (vagina), and the sun. Then: ĀṂ, IṂ, ĪṂ, UṂ—Vajrā, Gaurī, Vārī, Vajraḍākinī; ŪṂ, ṚṂ, ṜṂ, ḶṂ—Pukkasī, Śavarī, Caṇḍālī, Ḍombī; ḶṂ, EṂ, AIṂ, OṂ—Gaurī, Caurī, Vetālī, Ghasmarī; by the syllable AUṂ, Bhūcarī; and by the syllable AṂ, Khecarī.
Having thus produced them in sequence, one should visualize them as wrathful through the colors, marks, and other attributes of Nairātmyā, performing the *tāṇḍava* dance upon corpses.

Then, from the seed-syllables (*bīja*) at one's own heart, the moon disks and individual seed-syllables for the fourteen goddesses are emanated into the hearts of the [deities]. From the complete transformation of these seed-syllables and the ritual daggers (*kīla*), one should visualize the goddesses as before. *Āṃ*, *Āiṃ*, *Āiṃ*, and *Auṃ* are the [seeds] of Vajrā, Gaurī, Vārī, and Vajradākinī. *Āuṃ*, *Rīṃ*, *Rīṃ*, and *Līṃ* are those of Pukkasī and Śavarī.

Dang tzaṇḍālī and Dombinī, Līm Ām Āem ĀEem Ni Gūrī and Tsūrī, Betālī and Ghasmarī, Oṃ Ni Sa Spyod ma (Pṛthivīcāriṇī), and Oṃ Ni Mkha' spyod ma (Khecari)—having generated them in their respective order, visualize them all as being identical in color, marks, and so forth to Nairātmyā, performing the dance posture at the heart of the corpse.
As it has been said:
"Indra [East] is Vajrā, Yama [South] is Gaurī, and in the West is Vāriyoginī."
In the northwest is Vajraḍākī, and in the center is the Yoginī Nairātmyā; Pukkasī is renowned in the northeast, and Śabarī is in the southeast corner;
Caṇḍālī is in the southwest, and Ḍombī is in the northwest.
Gaurī should be at the eastern gate, and Caurarūpiṇī at the southern;
Vettālī is renowned as being in the fifth [direction], and likewise Ghasmarī in the north;
Bhūcarī is renowned as being below, and Khecarikā is considered to be above. Thus.

In which locations do they reside? As stated in another tantra: Vajra-Śṛṅkhalā is in the east; Vajra-Yamamathani is in the southeast; Vajra-Dākinī is in the south; Nairātmya-yoginī is in the center; Pukkasī is in the northeast; Śavarī is in the southwest; Caṇḍālī is in the northwest; and Ḍombī always resides in the north. Gaurī is at the eastern gate.
"STE" means "possessing form," referring to Lhori (Lāṭī). To the west is Betālī; likewise, to the north is Ghasmarī; below is Bhūcarī, and above she is held to be Khecarī—so it is said.

Thus, having surveyed the mandala as fully accomplished on all sides, one should—with the hook-like rays of light from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart—summon all the lords of sages in the form of the fifteen yoginīs by means of one’s entire being; then, having dispelled the obstacles with the female gatekeepers and worshipped them with Gaurī and the others, one performs the summoning and so forth with the mantras: *oṃ vajragaurī ākarṣaya jaḥ*, *oṃ vajracaurī praveśaya hūṃ*, *oṃ vajravettālī bandhaya vaṃ*, *oṃ vajraghasmarī toṣaya hoḥ*. Having performed the summoning and the other rites, [one proceeds].

Having thus visualized the maṇḍala as being completely perfected, one should summon the Lords of Sages by means of the light-rays emerging from the hearts of all [the deities] in the manner of the fifteen yoginīs. Then, the female gatekeepers should expel obstructing spirits, and Gaurī and the others should present offerings. *Oṃ vajra gaurī ākarṣaya jaḥ*.
Having performed the summoning and other rites with these [mantras]: *Oṃ vajratso rī phra be shaya hūṃ*, *Oṃ vajrabetālī bandhaya bāṃ*, *Oṃ vajraghasmarī be shyāṃ kuru hoḥ*.

As before, having presided over the eyes and so forth, preceded by the presiding over the body and so forth, and having determined the Lord of the Crown who is to be consecrated, there is the sealing (*mudraṇa*) of the [deities] of the [cardinal] directions and so forth in sequence with Vairocana, Ratneśa, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi; with Vajrasattva, Akṣobhya, Ratneśa, and Amitābha. There is the sealing of the guardians of the corners and gates in sequence: the sealing of the Earth-dweller (*bhūcarī*) and the Subterranean-dweller (*pātālavāsinī*) with Vairocana; and the Sky-dweller (*khecarī*) with Amitābha.

As before, one should perform the consecration of the eyes and so forth, preceded by the consecration of the body and so forth. For the empowerment, one should visualize the Lord of the Family upon the crown of the head; in that regard, for Vajrī and the others, these are Vairocana, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi. As for those residing at the boundaries and the gatekeepers:
Cittavajrā, Nityavajrā, Ratnavajrā, and Amitābhā; Bhūcarī is Vairocana, and Khacarī is Amitābha.

As before, the goddesses should bow down with their respective offering substances and their own lotus-vessels, and present them into the skull-cup of the Bhagavatī; [they should do so] for the other deities of the maṇḍala as well. And they should partake [of the offerings]. "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra that tastes the nectar of all the Tathāgatas. There, Caṇḍālī should play the ḍamaru drum. Ḍombī, clinging to the garment, acts the part of a man. And those [goddesses], having generated the vajra in their own secret places, should cause her to experience passion.

Having performed the worship with "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the worship of all Tathāgatas," one should praise [them] with "Tuhu pariveṭia joiṇi sātha," etc., and with "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the praise and worship of all Tathāgatas."

Then, with the *gūrvi* and so forth, the skull-cup is completely filled with the substances of self-offering. One makes an offering of the nectar to the Blessed One, and the other members of the maṇḍala also partake of it. Reciting *oṃ sarvatathāgatāmṛtasvabhāvātmako ’ham*, one should shake a small rattle with the *tsanda lī* gesture and embrace the form with the syllable *hūṃ*. Then, [the consort] is generated within the secret lotus.

Having offered with "Oṃ sarvatathāgatapūja-vajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham," and having praised with "You are completely surrounded by yoginīs," and so forth, one praises with "Oṃ sarvatathāgata-stutipūja-vajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham."

Oṃ, O Great King who bestows the bliss of the lotus, you who grant happiness; O Universal One who partakes in the four joys, hūṃ hūṃ, perform the task for me! Oṃ, O Vajra of great hatred, you who bestow the four joys; O Lord whose singular essence is the face of the sky-goer (khagamukha), hūṃ hūṃ, perform the task for me! Thus one should inspire passion. Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the passion of all Tathāgatas.

[Performing the vajra-embrace with passion: Oṃ padma sukha dhāra ma hā rā gsu khāṃ tsatur ānanda bhagaviśva hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ kāryaṃ kuru śvā me. Oṃ vajra mahādveṣa tsaturānanda dāyaka khaga mukhe kara so nātha hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ kāryaṃ kuru śvā me. Having thus performed the vajra-embrace with passion: Oṃ sarvatathāgatānurāgaṇavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham.
Thus is the samādhi called Maṇḍalarājāgra, which is the saṃbhogakāya.
This refers to the *saṃbhogakāya* nature, the supreme king of maṇḍalas meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

Therein, at the navel is a sixty-four-petaled lotus with the syllable *Aṃ* in its center; at the heart is an eight-petaled [lotus] with the syllable *Hūṃ* in its center; at the throat is a sixteen-petaled [lotus] with the syllable *Oṃ* in its center; and at the head is a thirty-two-petaled [lotus] with the syllable *Haṃ* in its center. Then: "The Caṇḍālī blazes at the navel and burns the five Tathāgatas."
And having visualized: "The eyes and so forth burn; when they are burned, the moon flows," one should arrange [the syllables] as follows:

*Ām* in the center of the sixty-four-petaled lotus at the navel, *Hūṃ* in the center of the eight-petaled lotus at the heart, *Oṃ* in the center of the sixteen-petaled lotus at the throat, and *Hāṃ* in the center of the thirty-two-petaled lotus at the head.
By joining the fierce *lte bar gtum mo*,
the five Tathāgatas are incinerated,
and Locanā and the others are likewise incinerated.
One should meditate on Caṇḍālī, as it is said: "By means of the blazing [of the fire], the moon shall flow from the *haṃ*.

Having established sentient beings within their respective gnoses through the rays of light from the seed-syllables at one's own hearts and through their respective emanations, one should withdraw them into oneself. The Lord of the Maṇḍala establishes them in the state of Mahāvajradhara; thus, untiring in meditation, one should recite the mantra: *oṃ a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au aṃ svāhā*.

Immediately thereafter, from the light of their respective seed-syllables, they each emanate their own manifestations. Having established sentient beings within their respective primordial wisdoms, they dissolve the mandala. Abiding in the state of the Great Vajradhara, the Lord of the Mandala, one should meditate while reciting the words that sever the continuity of rebirth: *Oṃ ā āḥ ai aiḥ au auḥ ri rī li lī ae aeḥ ao aoḥ am aḥ svāhā*.

The cycles of cessation or the cycles of wrath; the procedure for sprinkling during bathing; the procedure for tasting nectar during the meal; the procedure for passion during sexual union; and, having performed the nourishment of the moon at the crown of the head with the drops of the *praṇava*, when one is weary, one should recite [the mantra] preceded by worship and other rites.

Performing purification is done through the ritual of empowerment (*abhiṣeka*). Enjoying food is the ritual of tasting nectar (*amṛta*). Engaging in pleasure is the practice of subsequent passion (*anurāga*). As for fatigue, one should first refresh the body by having nectar drip from the *oṃ* at the crown of the head, and then perform the recitation of the mantra.

"Having emanated that which is called the Vajrasamaya," and so forth, was stated in this context. In the event of a breach of the *samaya*, by means of the supreme horse-yoga (*paramāśvayoga*), one should bestow the empowerment as before with the rays from the *viśvavajra* and the syllable *khaṃ*. By means of the yoga of the protection wheel of the Lord of the Vighna-enemies, one should slay Māra.

Regarding the impairment of the commitments (*samaya*) as they have been taught, one should abide in the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the Glorious Supreme Steed (*Hayagrīva*), and through the light of the seed-syllable *Khaṃ* and the various vajras, confer initiation exactly as it is. As for the subduing of Māra, one should establish the wheel of obstructing spirits and enemies.
This is the meditative absorption called "the Supreme King of Karma, whose nature is the Emanation Body" (*nairmāṇikakāyātmā karmarājāgrī nāma samādhiḥ*).
"Today, from the very nature of the nirmāṇakāya, there is the samādhi of the Supreme Victor.
Having drawn the mandala of the goddesses and having obtained pure merit,
by that means this Best of Victors shall ferry the world across the ocean of existence."
Whatever merit is gained from drawing this wheel of ḍākinīs,
by that may all living beings cross the ocean of existence.
May [the practitioner] swiftly become the Supreme Victor!
The *Nairātmyāsādhana* is completed. Oṃ.
The *Sādhana* of Nairātmyā is complete.

In the chapter that will be explained, or as previously stated, the sequence for the arising of the deity has been presented; therefore, the sequence of the *sādhana* itself is now written here. Furthermore, in order that the other *sādhanas* of the deities mentioned below may be easily understood, they shall be written here in their proper order.

As before, having relied upon the wheel [of deities] within the moon at the heart by means of its rays, one should perform the ritual up to the arising of the celestial palace—including the worship, confession of misdeeds, offerings, and so forth, as well as the meditation on ultimate bodhicitta, the protection, and the meditation on the *dharmodaya*—either according to the sequence of the fivefold manifest enlightenment or according to the sequence of the moon and vajra. In either case, through the transformation of the syllable *tāṃ* into a blue lotus, preceded by the radiation [of light], one should bring Vajratārā to completion.

As before, visualize the wheel of the maṇḍala in front of you by means of the light rays of the syllable *TĀM* imagined upon a moon disk at the heart; preceded by prostrations, offerings, and so forth, meditate on the ultimate bodhicitta and perform the protection. Then, within the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), below the tiered pavilion, take up the practice and manifest enlightenment.

Alternatively, by means of the Moon or Vajra families, preceded by the sequence of emanation and reabsorption from the transformation of the syllables *TĀM* and *utpala* and so forth, one should generate Vajratārā.
As it has been said: "And that was also spoken:"
One should visualize the goddess Tārā situated in the center of the maṇḍala of the Mothers,
possessing eight arms and four faces, adorned with all ornaments.
MA MO’I DKYIL ’KHOR DBUS GNAS PAR.
One should meditate on the goddess Tārā,
who has four faces and eight arms,
and is adorned with all the various ornaments.
One should clearly visualize [her] as having the color of gold, auspicious, a maiden radiant with the [major] marks,
possessing a great crown of four Buddhas, and born from the empowerment of Vajrasūrya.
Blazing with the marks of a maiden,
consecrated by Vajrasūrya,
and wearing the great crown of the four Buddhas.
Possessing the beauty of fresh youth, with swaying golden earrings,
seated upon a universal lotus throne, and adorned with a red radiance.
With golden earrings shimmering,
seated upon various lotuses,
he is completely enveloped by red rays of light.
She holds a vajra-noose, a conch, and an arrow raised in her right hands;

The Sadhana of Vajratārā: By means of the fourfold vajra-stage as before, one meditates on the syllable *hrīḥ* upon a sun disk. Then follows worship, confession of misdeeds, the meditation on emptiness, and the protection circle. Within the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*), from the syllable *hrīḥ*, there arises a red eight-petaled lotus. In its center, upon a sun disk, by way of the fivefold process of awakening (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*), she is born from the single fusion of the melting of a red utpala flower and the syllable *hrīḥ*. She has tawny hair blazing upward; she wears a garment of tiger skin; she stands in the dancing posture of half-lotus (*ardhaparyaṅka*) upon the heart of a corpse and a sun disk; she is adorned with the five mudrās; she has a necklace made of a garland of severed heads; and she has three red, round eyes.

Upon this, by means of the sequence of the five aspects of manifest enlightenment, [the deity arises] from *hrīḥ*.

From the syllable *auṃ* and *utpala*, through the application of emanation, one should generate Kurukullā. She has one face and four arms; her first two hands hold an *utpala* flower with its petals closed as an arrow and a blooming flower as a bow.

One should recite the mantra: *oṃ kurukulle hrīḥ svāhā*. Desiring to bring a man or woman under one's control, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, one should recite it ten thousand times daily at the three junctions of the day, while visualizing oneself in the form of the Blessed Lady, wearing red lower garments and a red upper robe. Thereafter, one should meditate on a red eight-petaled lotus in the heart, its stalk entering the *yoni*, which has evolved from the syllable *hrīḥ*.

On those petals, the yogi should visualize eight bees—transformed from the eight final vowels, exceedingly joyful and robust, recited in sequence, and impelled by the wind of their own names. Having emerged through the right nostril of the practitioner (the *uddīpa*), they enter through the left nostril of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*). Due to the forceful inhalation [by the sādhya], the yogi should see them crushing the vowels joined with the first and eighth vowels respectively.

One should recite: *Oṃ kuru kulle hrīḥ svāhā*. One who desires to bring under control a woman or a man should begin on the first day of the waxing moon; wearing red garments and meditating upon the goddess, one should recite twenty thousand times three times each day. Then, on the night of the fifteenth, [one should focus on] the *hrīḥ* at the heart.

Visualize an eight-petaled hollow red lotus that has arisen from the transformation [of the seed-syllable] and is inserted into the secret place. On its petals, visualize eight bees—red in color, wrathful, intoxicated by passion, and arising from the eight long vowels—which are driven out through the left nostril by the wind of the breath. They enter through the right nostril of the object of accomplishment and settle upon his heart.
One should visualize that [the bees] are intoxicated by the eight short vowels residing [within the lotus], and thus they become terrified and scatter in all directions.

Subsequently, with arrows whose tips are red utpala flowers drawn back to the ear, and employing the "confusion" (*saṃmohana*) and other mudrās, while reciting the mantra joined with the "gaze" (*dṛṣṭi*) and "fist" (*muṣṭi*) gestures, one should pierce the filaments. Then, those bees, impelled by their own *samaya*, emerge through the left nostril, seize each vowel one by one, and enter the yoginī through the opening of the right nostril. As for "in the heart," one should effect a state of oneness through the knowledge of one's own *samaya*.

Then, having visualized her bound at the neck with the stalk of a blue lotus noose and pressed at the heart with a hook, and as being filled with the flames of light-rays, he should bring her under control. The joyful yogi should recite the mantra while mounted upon a firebrand-wheel (*alātacakra*). Having meditated in this manner, he should recite the mantra.

Then, the yogin fills his ear-cavities with a bow of flowers and arrows of *utpala* lilies; fixing his gaze upon the navel, he strikes the heart-lotus of the object of accomplishment. Stimulated by their own respective pledges (*samaya*), those bees each take hold of the vowel-syllables, emerge from the yogin’s left nostril, enter through the yogin’s right nostril, and [merge into] his own pledge-awareness (*samayajñāna*).

Contemplating [the deity] with wisdom and non-duality, one should then bind the neck with a cord of *utpala* stalks and press the heart with an iron hook. Visualizing the mantra-garland as flickering with blazing rays of light like a whirling circle of fire, one recites:

*oṃ kurukulle hrīḥ amukīṃ amukaṃ vā vaśam ānaya svāhā*. Thus, one should recite throughout the entire night on the full moon day. Then, at dawn, she will arrive, overwhelmed and naked; of this there is no doubt.

If one recites "Oṃ ku ru ku lle hrīḥ che ge mo ba śyām mā naya hrīḥ svāhā" continuously from the time of dawn until the break of day, at the hour of dawn, a young woman and so forth will certainly arrive, intoxicated and stripped of her clothes.
Thus ends the *Kurukullā-sādhana*. || o ||
The *Sādhana of Kurukulle* is complete.

As before, having meditated on the syllable *Haṃ* upon a moon at the heart, one performs the worship, confession of misdeeds, and so forth. Some say it is a sword transformed from an *utpala* lotus. [The deity] has six arms, is in the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) sentiment, has one face, and wears matted locks.
One should worship Vajrānaṅga, who is sixteen years of age and yellow in color.
On the right, the hero holds an arrow; on the second [hand], he holds a sword;
on the third, one should know he holds a mirror; and on the left, he holds a bow.

One should likewise visualize [the deity] with six arms, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, as the second Indīvara and likewise Kaṅkerṇiparṇa. Having meditated as before, preceded by the entry of the *jñānasattva* and so forth, and having repeatedly contemplated the welfare of the world through the rays of light from the seed-syllable at the heart-mark, one should recite the mantra.

As before, having visualized a syllable upon a moon disk at the heart and preceded by offerings, the confession of misdeeds, and so forth, one meditates on emptiness. Then, through the sequence of the five manifest enlightenments, the seed-syllable and the sign of the sword completely transform, and one should visualize oneself as Vajra-ananga, with either four or six arms, yellow in color and graceful.

Visualize [him] with a lock of hair on his forehead, sixteen years of age, and adorned with the ornaments of youth; holding an arrow, a sword, and a mirror in his right hands, and a bow, an *utpala*, and an *aśoka* leaf in his left hands; seated in the posture with the left leg extended. Having inserted the wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*) as before, visualize that he performs the benefit of sentient beings through the light rays of the seed-syllable at his heart:
*oṃ mañjughoṣāya hrīḥ jaḥ*. [This is for] the sādhana.

One should meditate upon her heart; thus all women are brought under control.

One should frighten the woman with a sword, and then show her a mirror;

If one meditates thus, she will certainly be summoned. This is the *Vajrānaṅgasādhana*. Oṃ.
The *Kāyavajrasādhana* is complete.

Perfected through the wisdom of the syllable HŪṂ, he is the Vajra-holder Vajrahūṃkāra.
With both hands, he forms the mudrā through the application of the bell and vajra.
Generated from the syllable HŪṂ GI,
Vajra-Hūṃkāra, the possessor of the vajra,
through the union with the vajra bell—
With two hands bound in mudrā,
his body treads upon Bhairava with the pratyālīḍha stance;
having meditated on the Vajra family at his crown, one should recollect Trailokyavijaya.
With the posture of the left leg extended,
he dwells at the heart of Bhairava;
his crown is adorned with the Vajra family.
One should meditate on Trailokyavijaya:
Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā. The goddess,
arisen from the wisdom of the syllable Tāṃ, holding a boon-granting blue lotus as her weapon,
resembling a dark-green hue, is ever established in the auspicious state.
As it appears from the *Tāṃ gi yi ge las byung ba*:
"The blue-colored goddess,
holding the supreme [wish-granting jewel] and the utpala lotus."
Upon a seat of various lotuses, one should meditate on the Goddess Amoghadhāriṇī at the crown of the head—
possessing great passion and good fortune, and having the form of the syllable Tāra.
Abiding in the posture of eternal goodness,
adorned on the crown of the head by Amoghasiddhi,
for the sake of those with good fortune who have encountered great obstacles—
One should visualize oneself in the form of Tārā: Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture svāhā.
Oṃ tāre tuttāre ture svāhā!
[I praise her] who is born from the syllable Maṃ, who holds the boon-granting [gesture] and the Aśoka flower,
who resembles the rising sun, and whose hair is adorned by Śrī-Vairocana.
Arising from the syllable MĀṂ,
holding a supreme, sorrowless wish-fulfilling tree,
with a complexion like the rising sun.
The practitioner should meditate upon Māricī, who wears a crown of Vairocana, is mounted upon a chariot drawn by seven horses, stands in the *ālīḍha* posture,
and whose body is adorned with the sentiment of erotic passion (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*).
Upon a chariot drawn by seven horses,
with the right leg extended in the posture of sport,
she is graceful and adorned with ornaments on her limbs.
Meditate on the light rays of the one who dwells in concealment.
Oṃ māricī svāhā. Oṃ ārya-mārīcyai svāhā.
Born from the syllable *cuṃ*, with a radiance like the stalk of an autumn lotus,
holding jeweled palms joined at her heart, she stands in a graceful,
languid pose.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa,
she has the complexion of a child; holding a cintāmaṇi jewel at her heart, she sits upon a seat of various lotuses.
One should visualize the Goddess seated upon a universal lotus throne, her head perpetually pressed down;
one should contemplate the Goddess as overwhelmed, bringing forth the emission of the *bodhicitta*. She remains perfectly poised in the posture of eating.
Adorned with Vairocana upon the crown of the head,
visualize the bodhicitta dripping and flowing,
and perform the arousal accompanied by intoxication.
Oṃ cale cule cunde svāhā.
Oṃ tsa le tzu le tsun de svāhā.
She who is born from the syllable Vaṃ is Vasudhārā, of beautiful golden-yellow hue,
granting boons, holding grain in her hand, and seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture.
With hair atop the head of Ratneśa; from the syllable BĀṂ, the goddess Vasudhārā appears, golden in color.
Holding a supreme, medicinal sprout in his hand,
he sits upon a precious lotus seat in the vajra posture.
Rinchen Wangpo with a crown: Oṃ vasudhāre vasuvṛṣṭiṃ pātaya vasu svāhā!
*Oṃ ba su dhare bsu brishṭi pa tā ya ba su svā hā*.
One should visualize [the deity] born from the syllable *jaṃ*, who performs the act of paralyzing (*jambhana*),
wearing a crown of Ratneśa, and holding a citron fruit in his right hand.
In the left [hand], a jewel-staff;
one should visualize Acala arising from the syllable DZAṂ.
Adorned with all the ornaments of the gods,
holding a wish-fulfilling tree in her right hand,
and a precious basket in her left.
Rinchen Wangpo Codpan-can, oṃ jambhala jalendrāya svāhā.
Oṃ Dzaṃbha la dza lendra ye svāhā.

One should meditate upon Pratisarā, who is born from the syllable *praṃ*, holds a sword and a wheel, has Vairocana situated upon her head, gives birth to the form of Mañjuśrī, and stands upon the position within the maṇḍala.
Arising from the syllable Bām,
he holds a wheel and a sword,
and wears the crown of Vairocana.
Abiding in the posture of the squatting position (baddhaparyaṅka),
one should meditate on the form of a youth,
accompanied by the individualized atoms (anus).
Oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi mahāpratisare hūṃ 2 phaṭ 2 svāhā.
Oṃ mā nidha ri badzri ni ma h’a pra ti sa re hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā.
Perfectly arisen from the wisdom of the syllable *hūṃ*, he has two arms and one face;
he is black in color, possesses great radiance, and holds a curved knife and a skull-cup.
From the syllables HŪṂ, GI,
and YI arises the Great Black One with two arms, having one face and a deep blue complexion that blazes intensely.
Holding a copper knife and a skull-cup, wearing a necklace made of a garland of severed heads, terrifying with fearsome fangs,
having a dwarf-like form and great vital energy, he drips blood from his mouth.
Wearing a necklace made of human heads,
with a gaping mouth that is terrifying,
short-statured, and of great majesty.
Visualize blood dripping from the mouth;
whoever always hates the Master, whoever has exhausted the Three Jewels,
and whoever hates many sentient beings, is devoured by Mahākāla.
Those who harbor constant malice toward their preceptors,
those who cause harm to the Three Jewels,
and those who kill various sentient beings—

The Great Black One shall devour him! Oṃ Mahākālāśāsanāpahāri! This is the final time; this is that one who harms the Three Jewels! If you remember your vow, then eat, eat this wicked one! Kha kha khāhi 2! Māra 2! Gṛhṇa 2! Bandha 2! Hana 2! Daha 2! Paca 2! Dinam ekena hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ Mahākālāśāsanāpahāri, eṣo 'paścimakālo 'yam, idaṃ tad ratnatrayāpakāriṇam. Da ha da ha, pa tsa pa tsa, dinam ekena hūṃ phaṭ!

"Born from the syllable *hūṃ*" means transformed by the syllable *hūṃ*. "Constantly devoted to hatred" means inclined toward the destruction of duality. "With minds possessed by cruelty" means with a mind that is most arrogant due to its cruelty.

Regarding the phrase "arisen from *hūṃ*," it means generated from the complete transformation of the syllable *hūṃ*. "Always gone beyond hatred" means having reached the ultimate limit of non-duality. "The mind is inwardly wrathful" means possessing a mind that is arrogant with anger.

*Namaḥ samanta*—this is an indeclinable expression; its meaning is "everywhere," that is to say, "in every way. *Caṇḍetyādi*: it refers to the subduer (*parābhava*) of those who are fierce (*caṇḍa*), such as the maṇḍalas of Yama-rākṣasas and others; it is the agent (*kara*) of that subduing, thus "the one who casts down the fierce maṇḍalas" (*caṇḍamaṇḍalākṣepakara*). The mind, which is empty of the grasped and so forth, is *hūṃ*. Because it tears apart (*pāṭana*) the wicked, it is *phaṭ*.

*Na maḥ samanta* means "prostration from all doors," which is non-dual. Regarding *candhamandalakṣepa*, *candhamandala* refers to Yama, the rākṣasīs, and so forth. *Āṃ kṣepa* means "to cast away. Because one performs that [action], it is called *candhamandalakṣepa*. *Hūṃ* refers to the sound of emptiness through seizing and so forth.
"O mind without conditions! The syllable *Phaṭ* is that which causes the wicked to fall.

Regarding the phrase "the unblemished lotus of women" and so forth: "of women" (*nārīṇām*) is an elliptical expression; it should also be understood to include men. "Unblemished" means without holes or fissures. "Lotus" refers to the skull-cup (*kapāla*). "Of women" is an elliptical indication; it should also be taken to apply to men. "Lotus" is the skull-cup. "Without cracks" means without leaks or openings.
And so it has been said:
"One [face] is like the moon, a cow's face, or a lotus."
It should be known as having a human head and being joined with golden doors; it resembles a lotus, and furthermore,
it possesses golden gates.
The skull of a Brāhmaṇa and so forth, and the skull of one born of a low caste; each [skull] is increased by one ear.
The skull should be of inferior appearance with a hole above the ear; it should be known as a human skull possessing a single protuberance (*dum bu*).
The back of a bull is covered with humps, while that of a heifer is adorned with a dewlap; however, the back of eunuchs has a hollow, whereas that of women is always free from such defects.
The head is likewise to be known by the wise as being free from wounds; it is beautiful and without blemish,
to be understood by those possessed of primordial wisdom.
If there is a line like a string of pearls upon the forehead and above the ears, [he is a cakravartin].
One, two, three, and four segments; the sixteenth and the twelfth [are] the moon. 4.
One segment, two segments, three segments, four, the twelfth and the sixteenth.
Likewise, it is without cracks or flaws;
it should be understood as being like the moon.
The *gomukha* [vessel] should be white and red, slightly elongated, and very beautiful.
The lotus has the form of a lotus, yellow, red, and likewise white; slightly elongated and very beautiful, reddish-yellow like the face of a bull.
The lotus-like [skulls] are the lotuses; they are red-yellow and white.
One should accept the excellent skulls, but one should avoid those that remain [defective].
However, that which is defective— such as being cracked or split— is even more unfit to be accepted. One should discard what remains beyond that [which is permissible].
"The skull of one who has died from [diseases such as] gas or defilements is extremely difficult to grasp.

Regarding "by means of the application of the four vidyās": the four vidyās are Locanā and the others. Their "application" refers to the practice of summoning and so forth. "One should fill it with all the Buddhas" means that one should fill it, up to every single atom, with the circles of deities whose nature consists of the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the application of the four vidyās," "application" refers to the activities such as summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*). From among those four vidyās, the goddesses such as Locanā and the others should perform the summoning and so forth in their respective order. As for the phrase "to be filled by all Buddhas," this means that the faces, which are the nature of the deities, should be filled by the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*), [visualized] as being composed of the subtle atoms of the Buddhas.

Alternatively, there is the application of the four vidyās: piercing with the vajrāṅkuśa at the heart; the noose at the throat; abiding in the wind-maṇḍala; and sprinkling with the nectar-pitcher of the goddess upon the head. Regarding the phrase "by means of the ritual of the foot-dust": the "foot" is the seed-syllable of the heart; the "dusts" are the rays; their "ritual" is the emanation of the deities holding the noose and the goad.

Alternatively, regarding the phrase "one should apply the four vidyās," this refers to piercing the heart with a vajra hook, binding [the deity] by the throat with a noose, drawing [them] in by circling them within the wind mandala, and then bathing [them] at the crown of the head with vases of nectar by the goddesses. The "footprints" are the seed-syllables at the heart; "dust" is their radiance;
and the "ritual" refers to the deities who hold the hook and the noose emanated from that.

Alternatively, *padapāṃśu* means the dust of the feet; its preparation involves making an image together with clay from both banks of a river. Having stepped upon it with the foot—using the *ālīḍha* stance for attracting a maiden and the *pratyālīḍha* stance for attracting a man—one should write the mantra; the word "skull" (*kapāla*) is to be understood as the remaining requirement.

Alternatively, "the dust of the footprint" refers to the earth upon which the foot has stepped. As for the ritual procedure: one should fashion an image from earth mixed with the dust of the footprint and water from both riverbanks. Regarding the phrase "one should press with the foot and recite," in the case of summoning a maiden, one should press with the left leg extended; in the case of a man, one should press with the right leg extended.
The remainder of the text, "having written [the mantra] on a skull," is to be understood as follows.

"Tam" means that one should recite the Yamāntaka mantra together with the injunction. This is the summary of its meaning: having taken a praiseworthy human skull, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp upon its back; within the pericarp, one should draw an image of the target's eyes and so forth using saffron, *gorocanā*, or red lac; and in her heart, one should write the garland-mantra ending with "jaḥ," such as: "Amukīm ākarṣaya jaḥ."

"Yama-antaka" means the Slayer of Yama. "Recitation" refers to the chanting of the mantra accompanied by the exhortation. The summarized meaning of this is as follows: one who desires to summon a woman should take the skull of a young girl possessing the auspicious marks, and on the back of that skull, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with its pericarp using vermillion, gorocanā, and the blood of a centipede; then, at the center...
Having drawn the forms of the deities to be accomplished, such as Uṣṇīṣā and so forth, one should write the mantra garland ending with "AĀḤ KARṢAYA JAḤ" in their hearts.

Alternatively, one should write the mantra on the filaments of a lotus, on a heart-shaped image made of foot-dust and so forth, or on birch bark and the like; having inserted it [into the heart], one should recite it—this is the remainder of the sense. And that heart of her or of him should be [touched] by the soles of the feet marked with vajras and hooks born from the syllable *hūṃ* situated within the solar disc, while standing in the *ālīḍha* posture and performing the gestures of drawing in the left and right shanks respectively; thus one should recite the garland-mantra together with the incantation.

Alternatively, one should perform the accomplishment by placing the mantra written on birch bark and so forth into the heart of a reflection produced from the dust of the footprints of Padmapāṇi; then, marking the heart of that reflection with a vajra hook arising from the syllable *HŪṂ* at the sole of the foot, one presses down upon it with the left leg extended in the manner of a hook, while reciting the mantra together with the words of exhortation.

Having seen the female or male object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) being raised or being raised, or being impelled or being impelled within a wind-mandala arising from the syllable *yaṃ* by means of the sound *jhraiḥ*, one should likewise emanate a perfected vajra-hook from one's own heart, give the command, and dispatch it to bring her [or him] forth. One should then apply meditative absorption (*adhimukti*) to that which is being brought forth or has been brought forth by that [hook] in the proper manner. She will certainly arrive. Once she has arrived, an offering (*argha*) of excellent sandalwood water and so forth should be presented to her and to that wrathful deity. This is the method for summoning the body of yakṣiṇīs and the like, as well as human women and men.

Furthermore, regarding the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*): having extracted it from the wind mandala generated from the syllable *yaṃ* by means of the light of the syllable *jaḥ*, one summons it. Then, as urged by that [wind], one emanates wrathful deities (*krodha*) from one’s own heart holding hooks and lassos; having commanded them, they draw [the object] forth exactly as it is. As it is carried away by the wind and arrives, one offers *argha* water of sandalwood and so forth to those wrathful deities and the rest.

One should perform the rite of giving (*dāna*); by that, one will summon yakṣīs, human women, and so forth. For the summoning of men, one should use a human skull and adopt the posture with the right leg extended (*pralambapāda*).

Regarding "the meditation on the arising of the three bodies": the arising of the deity through the seed-syllable, the emblem, and the seat is the arising of the three bodies. "The wielder of the great staff," and so forth: he wields a staff marked with a white vajra. He crushes various gods and asuras; thus, he is the "crusher of various gods and asuras."

Regarding the phrase "by meditating on the three *skus* as the places of birth": one should generate the form of the deity by means of the seat, the seed-syllable, and the signs (*cihna*). *Sita-danta* means "white-toothed" and refers to the one who holds a white vajra and a lotus. *Bibidāsura āsura mardaya ti* means "crush the various gods and asuras. *Bhūtān nirmatheti* means "churn the spirits (*bhūta*), hungry ghosts (*preta*), *piśācas*, *yakṣas*, and so forth. The remainder is as before.

"Bhūta-da-ni-rma-the" means to subjugate beings such as *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, *ḍākinīs*, and *yakṣas*. The remainder is as stated above: "by those [beings] crowded with hosts of *ḍākinīs*. "With the majesty of the syllable *hūṃ*" (*hūṃkṛtāṭopa*) means one who has manifested majesty by means of the syllable *hūṃ*; the meaning is that his eyes are contracted with anger due to a frown of wrathful intensity.

"By the spirits, the flesh-eaters, and the ḍākinīs being agitated, one should perform the sealing with the syllable *hūṃ*. This means that for those seized by spirits and others who have been sealed, one should gaze while encircling a wrathful frown with the syllable *hūṃ*, accompanied by a wrathful deity, with the eyebrows knit together.

"By vajra-pressing" means: [striking] with a blazing vajra formed from two hands arising as *hūṃ*, or a blazing vajra on the two feet, or a blazing vajra located at the heart and throat; or striking with mustard seeds transformed into blazing vajras by the syllable *hūṃ*. "Then, bliss" means being established in one's own natural state.

Regarding the phrase "one becomes blissful through being struck by a vajra": "being struck by a vajra" means that one should visualize vajras arising from the syllable *hūṃ* at the two hands and the two soles of the feet of the yoginī; then, by rubbing and massaging [the body] and striking it with a *yungs kar* (mustard seed) that has been generated as a blazing vajra from *hūṃ*, one becomes blissful, which occurs just as described previously.

This is its meaning: Having established oneself in the Aparājita-yoga and performed the protection, one should meditate on a blazing vajra born from the syllable *hūṃ* upon both hands or both feet. Then, having mentally drawn out the rākṣasa or other [obstructors] from the body of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and having placed them between the two vajras, one should meditate on them being consumed by those flames and so forth. While firmly pressing and rubbing [the hands or feet], one should repeat the mantra accompanied by the command: "May such-and-such a person be liberated from the rākṣasas and others!"

Furthermore, abiding in the yoga that cannot be overcome by others, having performed the protection, one should visualize blazing vajras arising from the syllable *hūṃ* on both palms and both soles. Mentally drawing forth the demons and other obstructors from the body of the object of practice, one should burn them with the blazing vajras as they approach the hands, and then place them at the feet, crushing and trampling them.

Having meditated in this way, recite the mantra while uttering the exhortation: *āmuṣyakarākṣasāya te bhyo moḍaya*. Alternatively, perform the mantra recitation accompanied by these words of exhortation.

Alternatively, having visualized the Rākṣasa or others specified as the object of the rite (*sādhya*) in that very same way, and having drawn them forth and bound them, one should then render the object breathless. With two vajras of blazing light from both hands, the two sides [of the body] are pressed; and with two blazing vajras visualized at his heart and throat, he is being burned. Having placed [the vajras] at the heart and throat, one should strike him while reciting each mantra individually, using royal mustard seeds—which have the form of thunderbolts produced from the blazing syllable *HŪṂ*—that have been consecrated one hundred and eight times.
One should visualize his body being tormented by those [seeds].

Alternatively, visualizing oneself as standing upon the body of the object of accomplishment and identifying them as being those very rākṣasas and so forth, one binds them; then, one should contemplate that the vital breaths of the object of accomplishment are severed.

Then, press the two hands together with the vajras against the two sides of the target's body; burn the target’s heart and throat with blazing vajras generated by the syllable *HŪṂ*, and generate the King of White Mustard Seeds as blazing vajras through the syllable *HŪṂ*. Recite the mantra one hundred and eight times, and then strike each individual mustard seed while reciting the mantra once over it, visualizing that they are reduced to powder.

By this means, he is certainly [subdued]. By him, weeping compassionately, having produced conviction through such acts as breaking the branches of trees, [the victim] is released; or he becomes free from poison. In that context, he also indicates restraint by means of logic. In that regard, "vajra" refers to Vajra-rākṣasas and the like; and by them, there is the restraint of suffering. Thereafter, one who has committed a supreme evil—such as an offender against the Three Jewels—is restrained and punished, and then enjoined to enter the path to awakening. Because it is beneficial for the future, it is happiness. In this sequence, one may desire to cause others to accept [this method] by means of rākṣasas and the like.

The rākṣasas and others will be filled with compassion and remorse; as long as the branch of the tree has not been broken, they must be released from their bonds. Alternatively, "pierced by stones" refers to the capturing of the rākṣasas and so forth; by capturing the rākṣasas and others, the disciples are subdued and brought to a state of compliance. They shall become happy.
"Ba ni" means that after cutting off the transgression, one is established on the path to enlightenment; thus, one should be raised up from the state of downfall.

Furthermore, on either of the two dark lunar days (the eighth or fourteenth), by means of the Aparājita yoga, one who is enraged should draw upon the skull of a man slain by a trident or weapon and hung up, a terrifying figure born from the syllable *HŪṂ*—fierce with bared fangs, wearing a skull-garland, wrathful, with hair standing erect, holding a *vetāḍa*-staff aloft in his right hand, and threatening with his left. Having drawn this, one should write the mantra accompanied by the command, "Seize so-and-so! at its heart, using poison, powdered bone, and blood from the ring finger.

This is also the *Vajrakrama* (Vajra Stage). Abiding in the yoga of oneself as the Unconquerable One (*Ajita*), on the waning moon, under a fierce lunar mansion, one may kill with a spear, or kill by means of sorcery, or even kill with weapons; having taken the skull [of the victim], one should generate a terrifying and fearsome corpse from the syllable *Hūṃ* within a charnel ground fire, with its hair bristling upward.

Draw the face of the Vetāla with his body bound by a wooden yoke, his right hand brandishing a copper knife of a Vetāla and his left hand making the threatening mudrā. At his heart, write the mantra including the exhortation "Kill so-and-so! (*amukaṃ ghātaya*), together with poison, bone ash, and the blood from the tip of the ring finger.

In the second human skull, one should fashion an effigy (*pratikṛti*) composed of a lump of earth mixed with the dust from the feet of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), funeral ashes, charcoal, and water crushed by a vajra. Having filled its heart with a palm-leaf inscribed with the *codanā-mantra* written in poison, bone-dust, and the blood of the ring finger, and having smeared it with poison, salt, and black mustard seeds, one should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) and other rites for both [the effigy and the deity]. Then, placing a skull-cup over it to enclose it as a casket, one should visualize that very [effigy] being trampled underfoot.

Having placed [the victim] underfoot with a display of majesty, one should recite the mantra at midnight in a cremation ground; he will certainly be seized by that [demon]. In this same way, one may also cause him to be seized by fevers, planetary spirits, and so forth.

For the second Yangthopa [practice], take the dust from the footprint of the object of accomplishment, along with charnel ground ashes and cremation ash. Sprinkle these with vajra-water. Then, having written the mantra together with the words of exhortation upon a *teala* leaf using poison and the blood of one's own index finger, insert it into the heart of a clay image. Anoint [the image] with poison, asafoetida (*laṅtsva*), and *skye tse*. Thereafter, perform both the summoning and so forth.

Having performed [the ritual], one should visualize holding that [victim] in a charnel ground or similar location, placing the skull of the *graha* upon [one's own] head with the mouths joined together. At midnight, while suppressing it with conceptual thought and reciting the mantra with a frowning face, the *graha* will certainly seize the victim. This same procedure also applies for seizing those afflicted by epidemics and the like.

"Hulu hulu" means: "Carry, carry! "Mahāpadma" means: because its intrinsic nature is mindfulness (*smṛti*), it is like a lotus (*padma*) that is not stained by anything. "Amṛtīkuru" means: it is nectar (*amṛta*) because its form is liberation (*nirvṛti*) through the separation from the one and the many. "Viṣān" means: those who are like poison. "A" means: [the syllable] *aḥ* by way of the perception of non-arising (*anutpanna*).

"Hu lu hu lu" means "please, please. "Ma hā padma" means that because mindfulness is completely pure, one is unstained by faults, being like a lotus (*padma*). "Ā mr̥tām guru" means that because one is free from unity and multiplicity, one should experience the natural state of *nirvāṇa*. "Vi shan ā": here, "vi sha" refers to conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
"PA'O, AA LA LA" means that there is no arising by way of intrinsic nature; it demonstrates that things are indeed overcome by conceptualization itself.

"It draws forth the great poison" means that by the rays of light from the red syllable *hūṃ* situated upon the sun at the heart, one draws forth the poisons residing throughout the three worlds. "It draws forth the great poison" [means] that by the light rays of the *hūṃ* syllable abiding on the sun at the heart, the poisons dwelling in the three realms are drawn forth.

"Awakening the sleeping in that manner" means: just as in the *Garuḍatantra* and other scriptures, those whose nature is like the sleeping *kāmara* and so forth are awakened; so too, it should be understood, is this awakening by that same method. In that regard, having performed the *Hayagrīva-yoga*, [visualizing] oneself standing upon the back of Garuḍa in the sun, one should ignite the poison residing in all the limbs with the rays of the syllable *HŪṂ* placed upon the blazing solar disc born from the *HŪṂ* at the heart of the victim (*sādhya*), for the purpose of awakening it.

"Thus, one causes them to rise from their fainting state" means that, as it appears in the *Garuda Treatise*, one awakens those whose life-force and mindfulness have been lost. Furthermore, one should meditate on the yoga of the *kanthika* (neck-ornament) abiding in the sun upon the back of a garuda; then, having placed the syllable *Hūṃ* upon the sun arising from a *Hūṃ* at the heart of the one to be accomplished, one [emits] the light of the *Hūṃ* in order to expel the poison.
"Then, one should cause [the poison] residing in all the limbs to blaze forth.

Then, on the palm of the left hand, one should visualize a white eight-petaled lotus born from the syllable *paṃ*, in the center of which is a white *hūṃ* syllable emitting rays of light and flowing with liquid nectar; or a *haḥ* syllable situated upon a moon disk; or the six-syllable mantra: *oṃ hrīḥ haḥ hūṃ jaḥ sphur*. Then, reciting the garland-mantra (*mālāmantra*), one should repeatedly wipe the person to be treated (*sādhya*) with that hand, starting from the head down to the feet.

One should visualize that stream of nectar from the mantra held in the hand taking up the poison from all parts of the body; as it flows out through the tips of the feet, one should see it becoming blackened. Likewise, the rays of the mantra also take up the poison through the yoga of gradual descent. Having gone into the fire and other elements and abandoned the poison there, one should resolve that they have become white once again.

Then, visualize an eight-petaled white lotus arising from the syllable *pāṃ* upon the palm of the left hand; upon it, place a white syllable *hūṃ* accompanied by light and dripping with nectar. Alternatively, [visualize] the syllable *haḥ*, or *oṃ hrīḥ ha hūṃ jaḥ phuḥ* upon a moon mandala.

It is also appropriate to arrange these six syllables [on the body]. Then, with that hand, starting from the head down to the feet, one should visualize that the flow of nectar from the light of the syllables draws out the poison from all the limbs; finally, one visualizes the black color being drawn out from the tips of the feet. While reciting the mantra garland, one should purify the entire body with white light rays from the mantra.

Alternatively, having rendered the victim free from poison by means of a stream of nectar flowing from the syllable *hrīḥ*—white and placed upon his head—as before, one should visualize him with a white body once again. One should recite the garland mantra in both ways; he will certainly become free from poison.

Alternatively, one should visualize a white syllable *hrīḥ* at the head of the person to be treated. By means of the stream of its nectar, one should imagine that the poisons are washed away from the soles of the feet downward, just as before, while visualizing the body of the person to be treated as white in color. Repeating this again and again, one should recite the mantra of the garland. In either case, the poison will certainly be eliminated.

Alternatively, having inscribed the white syllables of the name of the person to be treated upon a white tablet, each interwoven with a white *hūṃ* syllable, one should recite the *mālāmantra* by means of that very yoga; or, while meditating on the white body of the subject as being cleansed of its blue poison by a profuse stream of nectar flowing from a white *hrīḥ* syllable placed upon its head—in either case, the person becomes free from poison.

If one writes the syllables of the name of the person to be accomplished, alternating each with the syllable *hāṃ* and coloring them white, and recites the mantra of the garland using that very same application; or, having drawn the form of the person to be accomplished and arranged a white *hrīḥ* upon their crown, one visualizes that the stream of its nectar washes away the black color of the poison—then they will likewise become free from poison.

Moreover: By inscribing the syllables of the name of one bitten by a *haṃsa* snake, each letter individually, upon a wooden board, together with the syllables *dhūmra*, *asita*, *sita*, and *pīta*, one may effect paralysis (*stobha*), attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), pacification (*upaśama*), and immobilization (*stambha*). One should bind the poison with the syllable *ṭhaḥ* preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ), and likewise with the syllable *haḥ*. The seed-syllable of fire (*raṃ*) causes paralysis, provided that these are applied according to the prescribed ritual.

Alternatively, one should write the name of the person afflicted by poison and the name of the object to be accomplished, alternating them letter by letter, on a leaf. Encircling these with the syllables *tha* and *āḥ*, and applying the seed-syllable of *ha* and *mi* according to the ritual procedure, it will draw [the victim] in with the color of smoke; with white, it will pacify; with yellow, it will bind.

The *vajras* are the wrathful deities (*krodhas*); their "mass" (*sandoha*) is their collection. Their "arrogance" (*darpa*) [is the subject]. "Oṃ Amṛtakuṇḍali" is the address. "Stirred up by the wind" (*mārutoddhūtam*) means raised by a whirlwind. "And of that, the dust of the feet" refers to the foot-dust of Gaṇapati. Having taken the name of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), having written it, one should place it at the end of the foot—that is, on the sole of the foot—of Gaṇapati, saying "Oṃ Amṛtakuṇḍali, [this is] the foot. One should either write it there or recite it.

Regarding the phrase *badzra sandoha barpaya*: *badzra* means "wrathful one" (*krodha*); *sandoha* means "multitude" (*gaṇa*); *barpaya* means "demon" (*graha*). Regarding *āmr̥takundali*: it means "bliss" (*sukha*). Regarding "fanned by the wind": it means being fanned and carried away by the wind. Regarding "having grasped the name of the one to be accomplished": it means writing the mantra interspersed with the name. "One should place the Gaṇapati beneath the feet" means...

The phrase "I am the one who performs the rites" refers to the mantra *āmr̥takundalin*. "One should inscribe it beneath the feet" means that it should be written at the soles of the feet or recited at the end of the words.

Regarding the expression "displaying the majesty of the *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* sounds," this is due to their being uttered loudly. Regarding "born from the samādhi of the Vajrāmṛta produced by *hūṃ*," this means that by means of the syllable *hūṃ*, one abides in the form-samādhi of Amṛtakundalin.

Regarding the phrase "one should recite with *hūṃ daṅ phaṭ*," this refers to reciting in secret and aloud. Regarding the phrase "one should perform the *amṛta-samādhi* with *hūṃ*," this refers to meditating on the swirling of the nectar generated by *hūṃ*.

"By means of the application of the wrathful mantra. In this regard, the application of the mantra is as follows: having drawn a great navel, a sword, and a wheel situated within a wind-mandala upon a cloth stirred by the wind using a pen made from the wing of a large crow, with a liquid mixture of wood and charcoal from a cremation ground, yellow orpiment, poison, and *ariṣṭa* leaves, combined with blood from the ring toe of one's left foot; and having written an effigy in its navel and, in its heart, the inciting garland-mantra interspersed with the [target's] name—

Having fashioned an image out of clay from a potter’s wheel, earth from a footprint, and earth from a crossroads, one should place it within its heart; then, having placed it in a hollowed-out vessel made of two skull-halves, one should perform the invocation and other rites.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the ritual application of the wrathful mantra," the ritual application (*prayoga*) is as follows: one should go to a cemetery and take the ashes of a person who has been incinerated while under the influence of madness, along with *ba bla*, poison, and the sap of *ni pa* leaves. These are mixed with blood from the ring finger of the left foot and applied to garments dried in the wind and so forth, using a brush made from the quill-feathers of a great vulture. [This constitutes] the wind mandala.

Draw a wide hub for the wheel of the *la gnas pa'i ral gri* (the sword-dweller) and, within that hub, draw the form of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*). In its heart, write the mantra garland interspersed with the name. Fashion an image from clay produced from the wheel of a potter, as well as dust from a footprint and earth from a crossroads. Insert a scrap of cloth into the heart of the image, place it inside two skull-cups joined together, and precede this with the rite of summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*).

Homage to all Buddhas! Homage to Vajrakrodha, the Great Fanged, Terrifyingly Fierce One! Oṃ Amṛtakuṇḍali, expel [the name] so-and-so! Hūṃ Phaṭ! Thus, empowered with this incantation and consecrated eight hundred times with the root mantra, one should conceal it in a temple of the Mothers, at a crossroads, or in a cemetery.

Recite one hundred and eight times the garland mantra: *Namaḥ samantabuddhebhyaḥ namo vajrakrodhāya mahādāṃṣṭrotkaṭabhīṣaṇāya | oṃ āmṛtakundali āmu kaṃ autsṛjata ya hūṃ phaṭ*. Then, bury it in a mother’s house, at a crossroads, or in a charnel ground.

Visualizing the object to be accomplished mounted upon a camel standing on a circle of wind, and subsequently being led toward the southern direction by a wrathful figure holding a staff in his hand, one will certainly cause [the target] to be driven away. The remainder is easy to understand. *The object to be accomplished is mounted upon a camel driven by the wind; visualizing him being beaten by a fierce figure holding a staff in his hand and being led toward the southern direction, he will undoubtedly be led away. The rest is easy to understand.*

Regarding "to Yamadaṇḍa": because he possesses a staff for inflicting death and punishment just like Yama. Regarding "to Nīla": by virtue of his blue color. Regarding "to Nīladaṇḍa": both by virtue of the color of his staff and by name. As for "YAMADAṆḌĀYA": *yama* refers to Yama and others; *daṇḍa* refers to those who kill and inflict punishment. As for "NĪLĀYA": it refers to the color of the body. As for "NĪLADAṆḌĀYA": it refers to the color of the staff; thus, he is addressed by name.

"Turū turv"—be swift! "Murū murv"—envelop all the wicked and slay them! [This refers to] one who has harmed the Three Jewels and so forth. "Impelled by the rules of application" means impelled by those rules of application. In that regard, one who possesses the yoga of the Noble Nīladaṇḍa should duly fashion an image using charcoal from a funeral pyre, anthills, clay, husks, human flesh, and the dust from the feet of those to be slain; this is done upon a cloth from a cemetery using a pen made of human bone, with a mixture of poison, blood, *neli*, *trikaṭu*, *ariṣṭa*, leaves, and juices.

Having drawn a fire-maṇḍala resting upon a double-vajra (viśvavajra) and having inscribed within it the name interlaced with the *mālā-mantra*, one should cast it into the heart of the effigy, invoke [the deity], and place it between two skull-cups. Then, becoming enraged and fierce for the purpose of slaying him, one should trample upon it with the left foot, chew stones, bones, and nimba leaves, and at midday or midnight recite the mantra accompanied by the command: "Kill so-and-so! Kill! Hūṃ Phaṭ! with a voice of wrath. Within seven days, he causes death.

*Turu turu* means "long, long. *Muru muru* means "do it, do it! *Sarvaduştān* refers to those who harbor malice toward the Three Jewels. Regarding the accomplishment of the collection of applications, this is the ritual procedure for the application: one who possesses the yoga of the Noble Blue Staff [Heruka] should take charcoal from a cremation ground and earth from an anthill.

Having fashioned an image from the woman’s [hair], her excrement, and the dust from her footprints, together with poison, blood, and the three pungent substances (*tsha ba gsum*), one should write the name of the person to be accomplished interspersed with the mantra garland upon a cloth from a charnel ground using human bone ink. Then, using various vajras, one should draw a sun mandala; in its center, having written the name of the person to be accomplished interspersed with the mantra garland, one should place it within the image.

Having inserted [the victim's] heart into [a skull], preceded by the rite of summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*), one places it inside two skulls. Then, having visualized oneself as the fierce wrathful deity Mahābala, at midnight or at noon, one stands upon a human bone and a lotus leaf, pressing down with the left foot.
Reciting the mantra with the words of the wrathful deity interspersed with "Amuṣya māraya phaṭ," one will cause death within seven days.

Even so, if [the goal] is not accomplished, one should go to a cremation ground at midnight, fashion a triangular fire-pit with the ashes of a funeral pyre, kindle a fire with *nimba* wood, and having first performed the invocation, visualize the King of Wrath (*Krodharāja*) in its center. Then, using a sharp weapon, one should repeatedly cut an effigy, starting from the little toe of the left foot; being possessed by extreme wrath and reciting the mantra accompanied by the command, one should offer it into his wide-open mouth with angry speech.
He will certainly die on that very night.

If even this does not succeed, go to a charnel ground and light a fire with wood from a *nimba* tree. In the center of that [fire], invite the King of Wrathful Deities (*krodharāja*) and visualize his face as being extremely wide open. With a sharp weapon, seize the little toe of the left foot of the effigy and, having crushed it, recite the mantra while uttering words of incitement.
If you offer this as a burnt offering (*homa*) with great wrath, he will undoubtedly die that very night.

In the month of Śrāvaṇa, Karkoṭaka; in Bhādrapada, Śaṅkhapāla; in Āśvina, Takṣaka is to be known; and likewise Vāsuki in Kārttika. These very same [nāgas] rain in due order starting from Phālguna and so on, under the name Ucchuṣmakrodharāja, because the bodies of Ucchuṣmakrodharāja and the others are blazing. "Of all the nāgas" means of the eight beginning with Ananta. "Strike the heart" is for the purpose of causing them to rain.

*Au Tzusma Kro Dha R’a Dza* is the name [of the deity], because he possesses an extremely radiant body. *Nam: Sarba Nāga Nam* refers to the eight classes of nāgas, such as Ananta and the rest. *Hri Da Ya Phyi La Ta* means "to pierce the heart" for the purpose of causing rain to fall. Regarding that, during the final month of summer, it is *karkoṭa*; during the first month of autumn, it is *śaṅkhapāla*. Autumn...
