In the middle month of winter, it rains during the *tākṣaka* [nakṣatra]; in the last month of autumn, during the *vasuka*. Likewise, it should be understood that rain falls sequentially in the middle month of summer and so forth.

What was previously indicated is now explained in detail: [The practitioner] possesses the great power of yoga with eight arms and four faces as previously described, or possesses the yoga of two arms and one face. In an unbaked clay bowl, using *nelī* juice, one should write the mantra of *Śūlinī* interspersed within an eight-spoked sword-wheel and an eight-petaled lotus in the center.

Having written the heart-mantra of all the nāgas and enclosed it within another shallow bowl (śarāva), having wound it with *nelī* thread, and having invoked and worshipped Śūlinī and the nāgas, and having given them the command, one should cast that bowl-enclosure which impels all the nāgas into a lotus pond or similar body of water presided over by nāgas.

Although it was taught previously, it shall be explained here. As taught before, one should abide in the vajra-samādhi of Mahābala, either with four faces and eight arms or with one face and two arms. Abiding therein, without spilling the contents of the skull-cup, one [should visualize] the nāgas—the mantra interspersed with the *śūlinī* mantra—within the center of an eight-petaled lotus at the hub of an eight-edged wheel of swords, moistened with the blood of a corpse.

Having written the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) and joined the two halves of an earthen vessel (*kha sbyar*), wrap it with blue thread. Then, having summoned the *nāgas* and made offerings to them, issue the command. Joining the two halves of the vessel used for summoning the *nāgas*, place it in a pond or similar location where the *nāgas* dwell.

Alternatively, having written a five-pronged vajra with ink upon a palm leaf together with the mantra syllables, and having visualized that very [vajra] as resembling a blazing fire, one should meditate upon Ekajaṭā as transformed from it—having two arms and one face, holding a flaying knife and a skull-cup, black in color, with a mass of tawny matted hair, and terrifying the nāgas. Having worshipped her and given the command, one should cast the palm leaf into a nāga lake.

Alternatively, write the words of the mantra of the five-pronged crossed vajra upon a palm leaf; visualize it as blazing with flames. From that, meditate on the goddess Ekajaṭī arising—one-faced and two-armed, holding a copper knife and a skull-cup, blue in color, with orange-brown hair tied upward and bound by three skulls.
Having made offerings and issued the command, cast the palm leaf into the ocean of the nāgas.

Then, in another secluded place, one should draw a fire-mandala and a wind-mandala, and in their center, a water-mandala; having drawn an eight-petaled lotus there, one should depict Varuṇa upon its pericarp—white in color, with seven fruits, human in form from the navel upward, two-armed, and holding a serpent-noose in his hand.

Then, on another empty spot, draw a mandala of fire; in its center, upon a mandala of water, draw an eight-petaled lotus. In its hub, draw the body of Varuṇa, white in color, with the upper body in human form, possessing seven humps, and holding a snake-noose in his two hands.

In the petals starting from the east, there is the dark blue Ananta upon the petal of a blue lotus; the white Vāsuki; the red Takṣaka; and the black Karkoṭaka. In the petals of the southeast and southwest are the pale-white Padma and Mahāpadma. In the northwest is the yellow Śaṅkhapāla. In the northeast is the multicolored Kulika.

In the directions beginning with the East are Ānanta, blue-green; Vāsuki, white; Takṣaka, red; and Karkoṭaka, blue. At the junctions of the South and the Southwest are Padma and Mahāpadma, both pale yellow. At the junction of the Northwest is Śaṅkhapāla, golden-yellow. In the Northeast is Kulika, of variegated colors.

Having thus drawn the mandala and generated all the nāgas with the syllable *naṃ*, one should present an offering of molasses, milk, and so forth, which is appropriate for the nāgas and consecrated with the *phuḥ* mantra. One should offer blue-colored flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, and banners, as well as blue jars filled with blue water. Furthermore, one should offer the powder of *sarja*, *tagara*, *kunduru*, *nakha*, white mustard seeds, and *nāgakeśara*; or even just the powder of *nāgakeśara* alone.

Having consecrated large incense with sugar and ghee lamps, one should offer them. Then, having summoned the *nāgas* by means of the syllable *naṃ* interlaced with the syllable *jaḥ*, and having caused them to enter their respective places, one should present the *argha* offering, worship them, and speak thus: "May you, O *nāgas*, send down rain; for our pleasure, by the command of the Blessed One. Thereafter, the *nāgas* should be visualized raining simultaneously. The mantra accompanied by this exhortation—*oṃ śūlapāṇi varṣāpaya śīghram | oṃ jyotirnirnāda varṣāpaya śīghram*—should be recited. Then they will rain.

Then, having performed the generation of all the nāgas from the syllables and so forth, one should offer the *naivedya* of the nāgas—such as rice and milk—to the deities who delight in them with the syllable PHAṬ.

While reciting the mantra, one should offer blue flowers, blue incense, and blue perfumes; as well as powders made from *tagara*, *uragasāra*, *kunduru*, *senaka*, white mustard seeds, and *nāgakesara*, mixed with sugar; and butter lamps produced from clarified butter—having consecrated these, one should offer them. In the same manner, [one should offer] the vases.

Offer blue water filled with blue water, and having inserted [the substance] with the mantra that intersperses the syllables *phuḥ* at the beginning and end, perform the worship preceded by the offering of *argha*. Then, say: "O Blessed One, by your command, may you, O nāgas, joyfully send down rain! Visualize the nāgas raining from the sky, and recite: *oṃ śūlapāṇaye varṣāpaya śīghram*.

If one recites the mantra accompanied by the exhortation "GHRAṂ OṂ DJO TI NIR NA DA BARSHĀPAYA ŚI GHĀṂ," rain will fall. Nevertheless, if there is still no rain, one should draw the maṇḍala of the nāgas in a circular fire-pit (agnikuṇḍa) in the same manner, invoke them, and meditate on the syllable *naṃ* upon their tongues. Having first offered the water for honor (*argha*) and so forth, one should offer three full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*) according to the ritual of fire-offering (*homavidhi*) using molasses and clarified butter. Then, with the mantra "OṂ NAṂ SVĀHĀ," one should offer as much molasses, milk, and so forth as desired. Thus satisfied, they will cause rain to fall.

If it still does not descend, construct a circular homa pit and draw the mandala of the nāgas therein. Having invited them, visualize the syllable *Nām* on your tongue; preceded by offerings such as *argha*, offer three libations of ghee mixed with molasses.
Then, offering a fire sacrifice (*homa*) of milk mixed with molasses and so forth, consecrated with the mantra *oṃ ānaḥ*, they will be satisfied and rain will fall.

Even if there is still no rain, one should inflict punishment. Having drawn a mandala in the sequence beginning with the north-west and the south-east, and having mentally stationed oneself in its center, one should—by means of a great power resembling the blazing fire at the end of an eon—crush the mass of the tails of all the nāgas while standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, or else with eight arms holding the Tārkṣya-vajra. One should recite this very mantra, interwoven with the syllable *naṃ*, accompanied by the command "Make it rain quickly," and chant the mantra with a display of majesty.
One should visualize all the nāgas in the expanse of the sky, overwhelmed by anger and fear and vomiting oceans of water; they will certainly cause rain to fall.

If [the disciple] still does not submit, they should be subdued by means of punishment. Having drawn a maṇḍala in the sequence of wind, fire, and so forth, one should meditate in its center upon the Samādhi of Great Power (*balavān-samādhi*): [visualize oneself as] a Garuda trampling the tails of the nāgas, with eight arms resembling blazing masses of fire subduing the nāgas, and accompanied by the internal recitation of the syllable *Oṃ*.

If one recites and brandishes this very mantra, expanding it with the exhortation "barsha ba ma sh'ighram" (quickly bring down rain!), and visualizes that the nāgas, terrified of the wrathful deity, fall from the sky in a state of intoxication, then rain will descend.

Even if there is still no rain, one should perform a ritual of sorcery against the *nāgas* in mild, moderate, or intense degrees according to this sequence: On a cloth from a corpse killed by a weapon or on a cloth from a cremation ground, one should draw an eight-spoked sword-wheel (*khaḍgacakra*) using poison, blood, black mustard, salt, and pungent oil; having drawn an eight-petaled lotus in its hub, one should write the eight *nāgas* upon the eight petals, each encircled by two *vaṃ* syllables, and write the syllable *vaṃ* in the pericarp.

Having fashioned an image of a serpent from earth taken from both banks of a river, combined with earth from a funeral pyre, an anthill, and the root of a single-stemmed tree, and having kneaded it with feces and urine; then, having inserted a written leaf into its heart, performed the ritual invocation (*āvāhana*), and smeared it with the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), black mustard seeds (*rājikā*), and so forth; having placed it beside a triangular fire-pit (*agnikuṇḍa*) and kindled a fire with wood from a cremation ground, one should heat it while reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times. Thereupon, they will rain.

If these do not succeed, then one should perform the wrathful rites (*abhicāra*) against the *nāgas* according to the distinctions of small, medium, and great [degrees of severity]. The sequence for this is as follows: on a cloth from a corpse or a cloth from a charnel ground, using poison, *ske tse*, *laṅ tsha*, black butter, and *tsa ba*, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus at the hub of a wheel of swords; on the petals—

On the [images of] nāgas, one should write the heart-mantras together with the syllable *pām* at the navel, interspersed with *hūṃ*. Then, from earth from both riverbanks, earth from a charnel ground, ash, earth from a fortress, and earth from the vicinity of a solitary tree—mixed with excrement—one should fashion effigies of the nāgas. Inserting a piece of cloth into their hearts, one should precede this with the summoning ritual and perform the three purifications.

If one anoints the effigy with human fat and kindles a fire with wood from a charnel ground, burning the image in the flames while reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times, [the target] will be brought under control; this is the minor [application].

If they still do not rain, then one should likewise draw a *nāga-maṇḍala* on the ground; wearing a blue upper garment and turban, or even naked, one should stand upon that maṇḍala with the left foot placed upon the upturned *nāgas*—who are presided over by a vajra situated upon a blazing sun—and gaze upon them as they are utterly overwhelmed by fear, filling the sky with the expansion of their hoods raised above their heads and turning the ocean into a sea of water with showers of vomiting blood. While reciting the mantra as before, interspersed with eight *naṃ*s, one should act with great majesty.
"O Nāgas, being urged by the command, 'Rain quickly under the weight of my wrath,' they will then certainly rain."

"If he still does not come even by that means, draw a nāga maṇḍala upon this very ground. Then, either wearing blue robes and a blue turban, or otherwise naked, stand in the sun. With your left foot marked by a blazing vajra, trample upon the effigy placed face down, and while pressing down with a wrathful gaze, split open its crown with the syllable *PHAT*. From the sky, [rain] blood..."
Thinking that [the water] will fall, as before, recite the names combined with the mantra including the exhortation "BAR ŚĀ BA YA Ś’EGHRAṂ," and by chanting the wrathful words, it will begin to fall.

If even so the Nāgas do not rain, then one should fashion an image of a Nāga out of poison, salt, black mustard, and *dhūtūraka*. Having driven a nine-finger-long stake of *khadira* wood into its heart, one should construct a triangular fire-mandala. Having brought either a Caṇḍāla’s fire or a cremation-ground fire there and kindled it with *phakāra* [fire-sticks], with one's body smeared with feces and urine and facing south, one should meditate upon Mahābala in the center of the hearth. With the tongue protruding far out as the syllable *HŪṂ*, one should [offer] into his mouth, whether individually or collectively, with wrath.

Reciting that mantra, one should begin at the tail with the left hand and, cutting it repeatedly with a sharp weapon, offer it into the fire. By performing one hundred and eight such offerings, they will certainly release a great rain.

If the *cchen po* (demon) still does not submit even by that means, one should fashion an image of the nāga out of poison, *laṅ tsha*, mustard seeds, and *da du ra*. A nine-finger-long *kīla* made of *śrīparṇī* wood is driven into its heart. Having kindled a fire of thorny wood or a charnel ground fire within a triangular *homa* pit, one visualizes the Powerful One (*Mahābala*) invited into the midst of the flames. Then, having smeared the body [of the effigy] with urine and feces, [one recites] the mouth...

Looking toward the south, one becomes very powerful; with the wrathful face expanded and the tongue blessed with the syllable *HŪṂ*, one seizes the victim from the entrance of the effigy and strikes them with a sharp weapon. If one performs one hundred and eight burnt offerings (*homa*) while reciting the mantra in reverse according to the ritual system, [the result] will descend.

If they still do not release [the rain], then it is the fault of Mahābala. Having fashioned an image of Mahābala out of poison, *rājikā* seeds, salt, and *dhuttūraka*, one should perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) and, using the *Śrīsumbha-yoga*, step upon it with feet empowered by the *vajra* while it lies face up upon a blazing sun. Then, reciting the mantra of four *huṃ*s accompanied by the command, "Rain quickly!", one should recite it ten thousand times (*ayuta*). Thereafter, Mahābala will certainly cause rain to fall.

If it does not flow after three such attempts, then by means of great power, one should fashion an effigy of the offender—along with their six siblings, their younger brother, and Da-dura—and summon them into it. Then, visualizing oneself as the Wrathful One (Gnod sbyin), one should trample the effigy underfoot with feet marked by the vajra while standing upon the sun, uttering the command "Shīghram" (swiftly). As for the intermediate stage: [the text continues with] the words of exhortation "Shīghram."
If one recites the mantra of the four *hūṃ*s forty thousand times while performing the *bhāṣaṇa* [invocation], it will cause even the most powerful [deities] to send down rain.

If, however, it does not rain, then one should visualize Sumbharāja with his mouth wide open, marked by the syllable *hūṃ*, within the *abhicāra* fire-pit. Having repeatedly cut out an effigy from his mouth using the yoga of Sumbharāja, one should perform ten thousand *homa* offerings with the mantra of the four *hūṃ*s accompanied by the words of incitement (*codanāpada*). By this means, the one of great power will certainly cause rain; this is the experience well-known to all yogins.

If the *kyang ma* does not arrive, then at that time, having invited the King of Harm (*gnod mdzes rgyal po*) into the pit for wrathful activities, one visualizes oneself as the Harmer (*gnod mdzes*). One strikes the previous image with the four-syllable mantra beginning with *Hūṃ*, accompanied by the words "tsinda tsinda," and performs three thousand burnt offerings; thus, he will certainly become exceedingly powerful.
It is well known that [the phrase] "rain falls" applies to all such applications.

For the purpose of bringing about rain, one should offer ten thousand oblations of ghee, milk, and so forth, according to the rite for pacification (*śāntika*), using the mantra of the powerful Nāga in a circular fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) whose mouth is white and represents the peaceful Vairocana and others. Their pacification will certainly occur. Śrī.

In order to expel the *cāra-ba* (sorcerers), the *nas-klus*, and the powerful spirits (*stobs-po-che*), if one performs twenty thousand burnt offerings (*homa*) of ghee, milk, and so forth, using their own mantras into a white circular fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) dedicated to Vairocana and others, they will undoubtedly be pacified.
In the event of excessive rain, [one should perform this] in the previously mentioned fire-pit for malevolent rites (*abhicāru-kuṇḍa*) dedicated to Śrī-Vajrasattva... [16 ff. missing].

If there is an extremely great obstacle, one will be severed [from it] by offering a hundred burnt offerings of old flowers previously offered to Śrī Vajrasattva and cotton wool into the sacrificial pit for wrathful rites as previously explained.

*Āt* means the meaning of suchness (*tattva*). *Ka na* means that which is observed by the intellect. *Tse ta tse ta* means that, like a messenger, it summons all commands. *Mo ta mo ta* means that by the force of the hand, it is joined with what is called "the mountain. *Tu ta tu ta* means that the weapon for seeing suchness [cuts] the long thread of ignorance.

Thus it is joined; here is the application: having drawn the images of Mahādeva and his consorts upon a human skull using the blood from the right big toe of a man, asafoetida, black butter, and the three types of *tsaba*, one performs the summoning while reciting that very mantra through the yoga of Vajrācala. By means of the application of the wind mandala, the lion—

Regarding the phrase "perform the ritual of expulsion": one visualizes that [the obstructors] are generated from *yāṃ* as winds and then expelled upon the back of a lion generated from *siṃ*, while imagining them being summoned by means of signs such as holding a hook and a noose. *Sumbha* is the vocative "O Sumbha"; it is called *Sumbha* because it destroys all obscurations. It is called *Sumbha* because it destroys them without exception. *Gṛhṇa gṛhṇa* means "seize, seize" [them] yourself.

*Śighra gr̥hṇāpa ya gr̥hṇāpa ya* means "cause others to seize [it] quickly. *Ānaya ho* means "bring it here! *Ho* is a respectful summons. *Hūṃ phaṭ* is a summons for the purpose of slaying; alternatively, it is a command consisting of four *hūṃ*s. *Phaṭ* is that which effects cessation. *Takkī hūṃ*.
Regarding this: *takkī* means "desire"; *hūṃ* means "wrath"; and *jaḥ* means "summoning. As it is said in the *Śrīparamādya*: "Takkī is always taught as desire; *hūṃ* is expressed as wrath; *jaḥ*..."

"Thus it is explained as the Excellent Guide. Regarding *oṃ siddha pātra*: it is the utterly pure *dharmadhātu*. Regarding *vimala*: it is free from the stains of the signs of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Regarding *śāṃkara*: it is because it has become a source of virtue for the enjoyment of the *dharma*. Regarding *pratyamgirā vajra*: it is that which overturns all that is improper.

Because it performs [the action]. *Tsiṇḍa tsiṇḍa* is to be joined with the mantras of others. *Bhinda bhinda* is to be joined with all mudrās. *Tziri tziri* is to be joined with the meanings of killing from the root. *Giri giri* means "to solicit. *Marā marā* means "make [them] invisible," that is, [the cessation of] the grasper and the grasped.

Through emptiness, the māras are equal to space. For that very reason, ten *hūṃ*s are uttered because within the dharmadhātu there is no distinction between object and subject. Three *phaṭ*s are uttered because of the downfall from the three abodes. Regarding the phrase "by oneself" and so forth: if one protects oneself, one dwells in the center of the protection wheel through the yoga of the Cakravartin Buddha-Usnīṣa, and then one’s own...

If one visualizes a *thig le* (bindu) of the syllable *Hūṃ* at the center of the heart-cakra—either as one’s own form or that of another—and visualizes it revolving counter-clockwise around the cakra, protection will be achieved; other [applications] are likewise so. Regarding the phrase "having held the vidyā in the arm," this refers to writing the syllable *Hūṃ* on the ten spokes of a ten-spoked wheel, writing the name at the hub, and placing the mantra garland upon the rim according to the oral instructions.

"Having written [it], it should be placed upon the shoulder. Regarding the passage beginning with "The Great Wrathful One" (*mahākrodha*), the term "essence" (*hṛdaya*) has the sense of "terrible" (*rma pa*). What is it? It refers to the mantras; those chapters in which they appear are so designated.
This concludes the explanation of the fourth chapter from the *Tattvavistara*, the Commentary on the Difficult Points of the *Vajrapañjara* of the Ḍākinīs.

"Then, [the mantra] 'entering the heart of Vajrasattva, O Blessed One who possesses the vajra' refers to all the deities of mantra. 'The Buddha-body' refers to the perfection of the body of Vajrasattva through the five stages of manifest enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*). 'Vajrasattva' refers to Śrī Heruka. Others should also be viewed in this same way. From the form of the Buddha, the mandala..."

"Maṇḍala" refers to the condensed maṇḍala; "lord" refers to the principal deity among those belonging to the maṇḍalas of the eternal ones and so forth. "Mantras" refers to the deities of mantra. Regarding the phrase "the wisdom and commitment [deities] abide in the heart," this means that the wisdom being (jñānasattva) is placed in the heart by way of the seed-syllable and the symbolic mark. "By means of the excellent application of the wisdom being" means—

The commitment maṇḍala and the wisdom maṇḍala are joined as one and burned. Regarding the phrase "having made the objects threefold," these are the objects of pleasure, suffering, and equanimity that give rise to desire, hatred, and delusion. "Abiding in the center of the protective commitment" refers to the yellow wheel with ten spokes generated from the syllable *Bhūṃ*.

"In the center where the ten wrathful deities reside" refers to the five mandalas, which constitute the condensed mandala. "Even by means of the powder divided into twenty-five" means that the threads should be gathered together. The twenty-five refers to the twenty-five aspects: for the Permanent One (Nitya), there are blue, yellow, red, green, and white; for the Sun (Sūrya), there is white.
Blue, red, green, and yellow; for Nṛtyeśvarī, white, yellow, and blue.

Jambhaka is green, while on the supreme horse [are] white, yellow, red, blue, and green. Heruka is white, yellow, red, green, and black; for it is said here: "In this regard, those who abide in the center are the Buddhas, the Protectors. Here, in order to demonstrate that the mind is the primary [factor], the summary...

Although it is taught that Hevajra himself is the principal deity of the mandala, this does not exclude others; rather, they should be apprehended according to one's preference through the stages of shifting the abodes and stabilizing. For that very reason, the colors of the earth portions should be apprehended according to the specific distinctions of the principal deities. "Meditating on each mandala" means meditating according to the sequence of each individual mandala. Alternatively, it may be condensed.

"PA'I DKYIL 'KHOR" (The *Pa* Mandala) refers to the condensed mandala; it is the meditation on five mandalas in which the five Universal Monarchs (*cakravartin*) occupy the central positions. "Eight by eight reside in the center" is an explanation of that very point: it summarizes the five Universal Monarchs surrounded by eight goddesses each. As for the placement of the gate-keeping goddesses at the gates, at that time [it constitutes] the condensed [mandala].

Regarding the phrase "it is the mandala," this means that the goddesses, such as the one holding a hook in her hand, are arrayed at the gates of the great mandala. Regarding the terms "fish" and "king": "fish" refers to the rohita fish, and "king" refers to the king of nāgas. As for the phrase "the supreme among beings, the realm of humans," this means that [it is] based upon the realm of human beings.

Those of the definite lineage and those of the indefinite lineage will attain the three types of enlightenment—both instantaneously and gradually—but others among the wandering beings do not, because they are deficient in their place of birth and their wisdom. For this very reason, the human realm alone is excellent. As for the phrase "having taken up the elephants and so forth," it refers to [the skull] in the right hand.

The meaning is that those who are afflicted are the disease, while in reality, those who are left [unafflicted] are the medicine. Regarding the phrase "the vajra that expels all diseases and brings them to complete pacification": because it brings all diseases to complete pacification, that which teaches where they are expelled from is called by that name. This concludes the explanation of the fifth chapter from the *Extensive Commentary on Reality* (*Tattvavistara*), the *Commentary on the Difficult Points of the Vajrapañjara Tantra*.

"The grasper of all bodies" refers to the grasping of all the deities of mantra. Regarding the phrase "the mind is recollection," and so forth, this teaches the recollection through the sequence of emanating subtle vajras after having emanated the deities of the mandala and attained the five signs. "Having meditated on Vajrasattva" refers to the meditation on Hevajra.

Regarding the phrase "Sealing with the Four Mudrās," this refers to the wisdom mind (jñānasattva) in the manner of the body, speech, and mind, as well as the seed-syllables and the signs. Alternatively, it refers to the lotuses at the navel, heart, throat, and crown of the head, which possess sixty-four, eight, sixteen, and thirty-two petals respectively, and are characterized by the nirmāṇa, dharma, saṃbhoga, and mahāsukha [mandalas].

On the great wheel, they are consecrated respectively by Āṃ, Hūṃ, Oṃ, and Hāṃ. The same applies to the [deities] such as Nityā and so forth. Thus, the one called "the king of hatred, Cha" is the Joyful Vajra (Hevajra). "The one who brings all hatred to an end" refers to the nature free from duality. One should meditate through the application of emanation, and the withdrawal is taught.

Regarding the phrase "PA STE," it refers to the emanation and reabsorption of clouds of one’s own body or clouds of signs from the *bindu* (drop), which is the withdrawal of the subtle *bindu* and the recollections (*anusmṛti*). "Indivisible from Vajrasattva" means that various vajras should serve as the crown ornament for the Joyful Vajra (*Ānandavajra*). Likewise, the constant [wheel] is the Dharma-wheel; for the sun, it is the precious vajra.

One should know that for the Lord of Speech (Mañjuśrī) there is a lotus, and for the Supreme Horse (Hayagrīva) there is a sword as a head-ornament. "Tens of millions of yojanas" is a symbol for the immeasurable. "The Buddha is the object of pride" means that one has conviction in oneself as having the nature of a Buddha. "Because one meditates on the luminous expanse of phenomena (dharmadhātu), by that [meditation], sentient beings become Buddhas."

Regarding the phrase "equal to space" (*dang mnyam ’gro*): it means that by meditating on the Buddha’s body as luminous and like an illusion, one becomes a Buddha itself. Regarding the statement, "By conceptualizing what is untrue, the mind is made defiled": conceptualizing what is untrue refers to the clinging to the notions of "self" and "mine," as well as to the subject and object. That itself is discursive thought (*rnam par rtog pa*), which consists of clinging to various diverse forms.

That very nature of the dependent other-power is what purifies the jewel of the mind. Just as that which is called "space" is free from clouds, mist, and so forth, it is free from adventitious stains. "Indestructible" means it is established by virtue of its natural stability. "Thoroughly stimulating the precious mind" means meditating on the meaning of truth. What, then, is external...

If it is argued that the appearance of things such as a conch shell and a water jar is indeed an observation of something existent—since an appearance of a lion arises in a place where a lion resides, but not in a place where one does not exist—the text states, "The jewel called mind is delusive," and so forth. The meaning of this is that, just as in dreams and the like, although there is no external object, the mind alone appears as an object; it does not appear because two [subject and object] exist.

"It is not the sun" means that he has attained sovereignty over the three realms; "the great dominion of the three realms" refers to becoming the lord of the three realms of the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*. "The heart-essence of Vajrasattva, most luminous" means that all phenomena are selfless (*anātman*). This concludes the explanation of the sixth chapter from the *Hevajra-pañjikā-tattvavyākhyāna*, the Commentary on the Difficult Points of the Vajra-Lattice of Ḍākinīs.

"Regarding 'we shall meditate on the one called Vajra,' this refers to the nature of the Dharmakāya which is like space. As for the phrase 'one should meditate on the fivefold form,' it means: the moon arising from the fifteen *ālikas*, and the sun arising from the thirty-four *kālis*—which are like stars containing all the qualities of the Buddhas—together with the bell (*ghaṇṭā*) arising from *Āṃ*, the skull-cup (*kapāla*), and the vajra arising from *Hūṃ*."

"The emanation and reabsorption of the wheels of the yoginīs, and the meditation on generating oneself in the form of the Vajradhara—this is what is meant by 'arranging the mandala according to its proper manner,' which refers to the emanation and reabsorption of the mandala deities from the body of one's own principal deity. As for the 'mandala of the four elements,' this refers to the mandalas of earth and so forth. Having visualized the Buddhas above that..."

The phrase "thus" (*zhes bya ba*) refers to generating [the deity] Vairocana from the syllable *bhūṃ*. "Indivisible" (*mi phyed pa*) means that all primordial wisdoms (*jñāna*) are indivisible and their nature is inseparable. By this, it is explained that the purification of the garland and water empowerments is the utterly pure *dharmadhātu* and the mirror-like primordial wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*), which wash away the stains of ignorance with their waters.

"Without arising and without ceasing" means being free from eternalism and nihilism; by this, the purity of the mastery over names is shown as the wisdom of the purity of the *dharmadhātu*. "Jewel" refers to the Buddhas. "The Guru of Gurus" is so called because of their unsurpassed great pride (*mahāmāna*). By this, the various jewels characterized by one's own self-mastery...

The purification of the crown of the assembly as the wisdom of equality is taught. Regarding the phrase "because of grasping the characteristics of desire and so forth," this refers to the Vajradhara who is attached to the *dharmatā* (the true nature) of phenomena by means of the discriminating wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*). By this, the purification of the vajra empowerment is taught. Regarding the phrase "bestowing the supreme fruit of accomplishment," it refers to the [wisdom] of... [activity].

It bestows the fruit of the meaningful primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) of the *ba nan tan* (vimala); through the melody of wisdom (*prajñā-svara*), it pervades all world systems without exception. By this, the purity of the dominant power (*adhipati-vaśitā*) is shown. That which is called the "vajra of the words of knowledge" (*vidyā-pada-vajra*) has as its nature the reversal of those [states of] ignorance. Regarding the statement, "The vase empowerment (*kalaśābhiṣeka*) is the first," and so forth, these refer to the three secrets.

"Having that nature, yet not being thus"—this means that the wisdom of the reality to be symbolized is not [ordinary] wisdom; for it is vast, untainted, and arises continuously. Regarding the term "vajra seed," the *vajras* are the Tathāgatas, and the "seed" is that which has become the form of the melted [deity].
"PA'O" refers to the individual mantras of the various families. This concludes the explanation of the seventh chapter from the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara-pañjikā-tattvavistara*.

"O Vajra Hatred, you are of the nature of the exhaustion of duality; because you destroy [it], you are 'Hatred. 'Pure Mind' means that all obscurations have been exhausted. 'Vajra Delusion' means not knowing [things] as dualistic. 'Pure Body' means being adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor signs."

For this reason, regarding the term "sublime discernment" (*samyak-pravicaya*): the "sublime" (*dam pa*) refers to the Buddhas; "discernment" (*so sor rtog pa*) is the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā-jñāna*). Regarding the phrase "with the forms of all Buddhas," it means that they manifest the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) through formless forms. Regarding the phrase "the Great Seal" (*mahāmudrā*) and so forth: if [it were] impure by its own inherent nature...

"Even 'gaṅ' (that which) does not exist. Regarding the thought, "What is purified by what? How is it purified?", it says: "When there is no contradictory entity," and so forth. A "contradictory entity" refers to an impure entity. The word "when" (*yadā*) is used with reference to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). At that time, the phrase "it should be purified" refers to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

This refers to being brought under control; it means that within the relative truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there is the possibility of purifying stains—such as the turbidity of water or a gem—through practices like purification. As for the term "wheel" (*cakra*), it refers to the wheel of the maṇḍala, which is the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*). If one asks, "How then is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) to be apprehended? it says, "One meditates on the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as mere suchness," and so forth. Here, the word "mere" (*tsam*)...

"Activity" (*bya ba*) refers to the thorough cutting off of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). "Meditating" (*rnam par bsgom pa*) means meditating on the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) as the body of one's own deity; it is meditating on [the deity] as a single body. "If one analyzes, the nature of reality is not a truly existent entity" means that "true" (*bden pa*) refers to the entity of suchness (*tattva*). "Analyzing" (*rnam par dpyad na*) means reflecting upon characteristics such as dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). "Existing" (*yod pa*)...

The phrase "it is not so" refers to the analysis of duality. Regarding the statement, "the movement of the world cannot be conceived," "the world" refers to the Buddhas, and "movement" refers to primordial wisdom (*jñāna*); it "cannot be conceived" because it is the domain of the inconceivable. The term "Mātṛ-maṇḍala" refers to the wheel of yoga. As for the "four faces," [this refers to] the central face...

"Yellow Maṇi": thereafter, one should arrange the female gatekeepers; this refers to the arrangement of the female staff-bearers (*lakuśī*), the female drummers (*lakuṭī*), and so forth. "Below, one should clearly visualize Hārītī": her color is blue. "The Uṣṇīṣavijayā": her color is yellow. "Tāre": she who delivers one from saṃsāra. Regarding "Tuttāre," *tuta* signifies... [definitively].

In the manner of a father’s word, it would be called "Khyod" (Thou), meaning "one who has gone alone"; "Tāre" is Tārā; "Tu-ra" means that which satisfies by enjoying all phenomena; "the seed-syllable of Caṇḍa" refers to the seed-syllable of birth; "Vajra-water" refers to semen; "Vajra-sun" refers to the uterine blood; "Supreme Horse" refers to human flesh; "Pi..."

*Tzu pi tzu* means "extremely subtle distraction"; because it is analogous to a fine cotton cloth, it is the wisdom that penetrates subtly. *Dzva la dzva la* means "that very [wisdom] itself," because the mind is luminous. *Dhi ri dhi ri* means "steadfast," which is unimpaired mindfulness. Regarding the phrase "the way of worldly conduct," *lugs* refers to "abiding," meaning by way of the ordinary manner.

"Abiding in the New Year," "Supreme" means "Excellent. Regarding the phrase "together with those branches of enlightenment," the "branches of enlightenment" refers to the maidens. The word "ho" can mean "for what reason" or "itself"; thus, worship performed by means of the very branches of enlightenment, together with the hand-mudrās such as the *lāsyā* (the graceful one), is "excellent"—that is, reality itself.

"Because it is the Teacher," and "two parts are cast from the Brahma-line" means that half of the gate is excluded. "Six parts" refers to six divisions. "Two parts of the gate are cast out" means the measure of two gates. Regarding the statement, "If two gates are raised by eight parts, what need is there to mention nine? this refers to the mandala of nine, where the space between two gates is demarcated; thus, "nine parts" is mentioned. Nine parts.

Thus ends the ninth chapter. This concludes the explanation of the eighth chapter from the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara-pañjikā-tattvavistara* (The Detailed Commentary on the Reality of the Vajra-Fence of the Ḍākinīs).

"Vidyādhara" means one who is radiant with ornaments such as fine garments and a topknot, and who possesses a mind endowed with loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth. "By the application of the right leg extended" means first, that it should be made comfortable from the outside. "By the application of the vajra-fist" means that one should form the vajra-bind (*vajrabandha*) with both hands at the chest (*kaṭaka*). *Vajrasattva*...

Reciting "DZA: DZA," one draws back the two middle fingers like a hook and strikes the ring and middle fingers together. "Vajra Letter" refers to whichever seed-syllable *Yāṃ* it may be. "Vajra Mandala" refers to the wind mandala. "Vajra Embracing" refers to the fire mandala arising from the seed-syllable *Rī*. "Vajra Frown" refers to...
The nectar should be ripened by means of a vajra marked with the syllable ĀṂ, which is generated by the syllable HŪṂ abiding upon the sun.

"Abiding in the center of the expanse of space" means abiding within the hollow of space. "The city of the source of phenomena" (*dharmodaya*) means abiding upon the fire-maṇḍala in the lotus of the consort, who is one's own light. "The yellow vajra" refers to one's own wrathful vajra. The remainder should be understood from the mouth of the Guru. "Du ra du ra" means "one breath."
*Tztsinda tztsinda* means "to clarify that very [reality]"; *hūṃ* means "definitive destruction."

*Dara* means "teaching" (*śāsana*). *Dāraya* means "explanation" (*vyākhyāna*). *Duṣṭānām mardaya mardaya* means "crush those who are wicked, making them invisible by means of the vajra-gaze. *Vajradhrīka* refers to grasping that very nature of non-dual primordial wisdom (*advayajñāna*). Furthermore, as stated in the *Guhyasamāja*: "That which is known through the five causes is expressed by the term 'vajra'; [it is] *dhrīka*..."

"It is explained that the objects are the *bya ba* (actions), while consciousness is asserted to be the *rdo rje 'dzin pa* (Vajradhara). Thus it was said. In this context, "causes" refers to the apprehended objects (*gzung ba*). "Cognitions" refers to the apprehending subjects (*'dzin pa*). "Five" means five times five, which is ten. "Vajra" means that these are condensed into the single nature of the mind. "Apprehending" means by way of the nature of that non-dual primordial wisdom (*ye shes*).

*Dzin pa'o* (The grasper), called *rnam shes* (consciousness), refers to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), specifically the untainted collection of consciousnesses of the Buddhas. *Vajranāma* is the name; its *samaya* is the vision [arising] from affection for all sentient beings who are to be disciplined. *Hu lu hu lu* means "to go," signifying that one has entered the unsurpassed path. *Āḥ*.

Regarding the term *āli-krīḍa*, it is also stated in that very *Guhyasamāja*: "Because all things in every way Are characterized by the characteristic of the symbol, All those such as the player (*krīḍaka*) Are explained as *āli-krīḍa*. In this context, "all" refers to the player, which is the perception (*saṃjñā*). "Of all" refers to that which is played with, namely, the objects to be symbolized.

"Kuṃ" means the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), which is the internalization of perception (*saṃjñā*). If one asks what kind of perception it is, it is stated as "Ārolika" in order to demonstrate the internalization of the signless (*animitta*). According to the method of definitive terminology, "Ā" refers to the self (*ātman*), the enjoyer; "Ro" refers to that which makes the mark; and "li kra" refers to the internalization of the characteristic. Śa...

*Śvā ta* means "name. *Parama-śvā ta* means "supremely eternal," which refers to entering the retinue of the Saṃbhogakāya. *Ā hye hi* means "come hither! *Dzina dzika* is as explained in the *Guhyasamāja*: "That which transcends existence and non-existence, arising from the elements and their derivatives, is the body of all sentient beings."

Regarding this, it is said: "The Victorious One taught that phenomena arise from [the union of] *jina* and *jindakrā*. In this context, "existent" (*yod pa*) refers to external objects that have become sentient beings and to arising; "non-existent" (*med pa*) refers to internal grasping and cessation; and "the middle" (*dbus*) refers to the interval and abiding—[phenomena] are free from these. If one asks what they are, it is said: "Arising from the primary elements and derived from the primary elements," which means they are untainted (*anāsrava*).

The aggregate of the form of the Father; "all sentient beings" refers to the Buddhas; "body" refers to the secret body; "generation" refers to birth; "Victorious One" (Jina) is a definitive designation, and by way of the method of definitive terminology, *jina* becomes *dzina*. *Vajrasūrya* is the name. *Tomo vidyāyana* refers to the various openings of the seal (*mudrā*).

It dispels the darkness of the six realms. *Samaya stvām hāṃ* means that [the deity] possesses the nature of the equality of all Buddhas. Regarding *ratnadhṛka*, it is stated in the commentary on the *Guhyasamāja*: "Because all meanings arise from it, the mind is explained as 'jewel' (*ratna*). Since the Knower of Awareness knows through that, the feeling is asserted to hold the jewel. Thus it is said.

That which is called "mind" (sems) is the nature of mind itself (cittatā). What is it like? Since all objects arise from it, it arises as the single flavor of the qualities of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. That very [nature] is awareness (vidyā); it is the knower of suchness (tattva). "Certainty" means that which is infallible. "Lineage" (rigs) means experience; it is the object of feeling, the natural state of the mind. Feeling is the awareness of equality.

This is the nature of *pa*. According to the method of definitive terminology, it is *ratnadhṛka*. As for *phu phu phu hi hi hi*, these are the natural sounds of a horse. Alternatively, *phu* means to emanate and soar; *hi* means to move like a horse, which refers to moving through all the coiled bodies (*sarpa-śarīra*). Regarding *prajñādhṛka*, according to the explanation in the *Guhyasamāja*, it is—*rab tu*... [the rest of the passage follows].

It is said: "Because consciousness is luminous, it is expressed as *prajñā*; because the mind grasps through formations (*saṃskāra*), wisdom is expressed as 'the grasper'. In this context, "luminous" means naturally radiant. What is it that is [luminous]? It is consciousness. By way of etymological definition, *jñā* refers to consciousness, while *pra* refers to luminosity. Formations...

That which is called "this" (*cetasa*) is the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). What is it like? It is the contemplation of reality (*tattva*) with diligence and reverence by the Buddhas. This concludes the explanation of the ninth chapter from the *Vajrajāla-pañjikā-tattvavistara* (The Detailed Commentary on Reality of the Vajra Net of Ḍākinīs).

"By means of the vajra eye" refers to the unobstructed vision. "By means of a network of various miraculous powers" refers to miraculous powers endowed with superior resolve (*adhimukti*), direct orientation, and the absence of volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*). In that regard, "superior resolve" is when sentient beings [perceive] the form of a Buddha, and Buddhas likewise [perceive] the bodies of sentient beings as non-differentiated.

"Intent on the auspicious" means that from the sky, he displays the treasury and so forth. "Without manifest effort" means that he displays birth, awakening, the turning of the wheel of Dharma, and so forth, as being spontaneously accomplished. This concludes the explanation of the tenth chapter from the *Tattvavistara*, the Commentary on the Difficult Points of the *Vajrajāla-dākinī*.

"Peaceful mind" refers to a mind of supreme clarity. "Empowerment" refers to abiding in the deity yoga of Vairocana and others, who are white in color; having subdued diseases such as those resembling a mouse, one performs the rite at one's own heart or within the lotus of wisdom, placing it upon a water mandala, and [bestows] the nectar held in a white flask.

Having conferred the continuous empowerment, one should visualize the divine body (*devatā-vigraha*) constructed from the subtle atoms of all the Buddhas. What is called the "mind of expansion" is the mental faculty (*manas*). Furthermore, here, through the yoga of the Vajrasūrya, for the sake of the practitioner abiding in the mandala of Mahendra, the conferral of empowerment by the stream of water from a yellow vase is as before. This is what is called the "subsequent mind of attachment."

The "mind of pride" refers to abiding in yogas such as that of the Lord of Dance (Nṛtyeśvara) and so forth; the conferral of empowerment by the stream of water from a red *kalaśa* is as before. The "cruel mind" (*gdug pa'i sems*) means a cruel, non-cruel, and intolerant—that is, an unbearable—mind. Fire is extinguished by the rain from a mass of clouds.
This concludes the explanation of the eleventh chapter from the *Vajrajāla-pañjikā-tattvavistara* (The Detailed Commentary on the Reality of the Vajra Net).

"Mount Sul Tsang Tsing" refers to the hermitage situated on the mountain slope; alternatively, because it does not waver from tasting the bodhicitta, "mount Sul" is wisdom (*prajñā*), and "Tsang Tsing Cave" is the lotus that has entered into the source of its phenomena (*dharmodaya*). Regarding the phrase "adorned with flowers, fruits, and so forth": "flowers" are past karma, and "fruits" are the body of this present life—the ripened result (*vipāka*).

Because it is [so], or else because it is like flower-pollen, and so forth—by these [examples], the teeth and so on are to be grasped. Regarding the phrase "the mind of awakening" (*bodhicitta*) and so forth, one might wonder: "How can the ultimate mind of awakening exist when entities such as the grasped and the grasper have been analyzed? Thinking thus, he says: "When analyzing whether entities are true or false," and so on.

When analyzed through reasoning, since it is untenable for there to be the very entities of apprehended object and apprehending subject, the meaning is that they are unreal and only the mind alone remains. If it is argued that although external entities such as the apprehended object are untenable, consciousness itself exists substantially, [the author] states: "By this application of non-arising," and so forth, regarding the one and the many.

Just as this preparation of the Sog-pa (Mongols) contradicts the existence of external objects, it likewise contradicts [the existence of] consciousness; here, there is nothing whatsoever that is established in equanimity or exists as an ultimate reality. "This birth" means it is empty—that is, it arises with the nature of emptiness. Regarding "Oṃ" and so forth: "Oṃ" is the meaning.

*Āḥ*. *Śūnyatā-jñāna* (the wisdom of emptiness) is so called because it is not merely luminosity; *vajra* means that because its nature is indivisible, it destroys all obscurations. Alternatively, the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) whose meaning is emptiness is *oṃ*; the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*) is *śūnyatā*; the discriminating wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) is *jñāna*; [the all-accomplishing wisdom is... *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*.

The gnosis of emanation (*nirmāṇa-jñāna*) is *vajra*, because the nirmāṇakāya remains as long as space exists. The gnosis of utter purity (*suviśuddha-jñāna*) is the *svabhāva-ātmaka* (the nature of intrinsic being). What is called "the union of immortality" refers to abiding in the yoga of the obstructors and enemies within the protection wheel. The "vajra mandala" is the wind mandala; the "mandala of light" is the mirror-like [wisdom].

The *gi dkyil 'khor* is the mandala of the ḍākinīs; the *mkha' 'gro'i dkyil 'khor* is the mandala of Hevajra; that which is called the "earth portion" is the mandala of Nairātmyā. This concludes the explanation of the twelfth chapter from the *Tattvavistara*, the difficult commentary on the *Vajrajāla-ḍākinī*.

"Kriyātantra is so called because it focuses externally on deities such as Umā and emphasizes practices such as ritual purity and silence. Kriyā-yoga is the focusing [of the mind] externally, away from oneself. Yoga is the focusing on the identity of one's own sovereign wheel of wisdom (*cakravartin*) and the self as one taste. Yogottara is..."

It is the practice of the great secret of supreme joy arising from the union with one’s own awareness (*svavidyā*). What is called "Unsurpassed Yoga" (*anuttarayoga*) refers to focusing upon the supreme bliss born from the union of one’s own deity’s vajra and lotus. Regarding the phrase "the inseparability of emptiness and compassion," emptiness is the characteristic of the absolute non-existence of duality; it is the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). That...

"Self-nature" (*nyid*) refers to synonyms such as "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*) and "suchness" (*tathatā*). "Compassion" (*karuṇā*) is the divine maṇḍala that comprises the five perfections (*pāramitā*); [the subject] has become of one taste, inseparable from that. Regarding this, either two syllables joined with the *hūṃ* of the causal Vajradhara may be inserted, or it is also appropriate for the two bodies (*kāya*) to be inserted; within the lotus at the navel is the fire of passion.

The nature of the two bodies (*kāya*) that arise from the request for empowerment is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The compassion (*karuṇā*) that benefits sentient beings through the light rays emanating from that [emptiness] is the essence of the divine body inseparable from it. This concludes the explanation of the thirteenth chapter from the *Tattvavistara*, the commentary on the difficult points of the *Vajrajāla* Ḍākinī.

Regarding the phrase "The Sphere of Excellent Conduct" (*Bhadra-gocara*): "Excellent" (*bhadra*) refers to the accomplishments (*siddhi*) such as those of *rīlu* and so forth; "sphere of conduct" (*gocara*) refers to the practice, meaning the means of accomplishment. "Vajra" refers to Hevajra. As for the "three families," the certainty taught elsewhere is applied here: "The Moon, the Excellent One, the Hare-marked [Moon], and the Radiant Ones—these three and four are the number of the Vedas."

From the *Kyiman* [tradition] onwards, the mountain body should be drawn with the qualities of the Sage [Buddha] numbering as many as arrows, together with the *ratna*. Alternatively, as stated elsewhere: "Gold, silver, and likewise copper, from fire, arrow, and the pair onwards—sixteen, three, and six respectively—with the *ol-se*, the mountain body is drawn thickly. It is just as it has been said. [The Naga King...]

"Thus it is said" refers to the two-headed emanation. "Seed" refers to the semen. "Vajra finger" refers to fingers shaped like an elephant's trunk and so forth. "Vajra tongue" refers to the tongue marked with the *hūṃ* syllable and the vajra. "Vajrasattva" refers to one's own [secret] mark. "Vajra embrace" refers to firmly clasping the neck. "Vajra heart..."

"Po" refers to indivisible bliss. "Lotus of attachment" means being endowed with the vajra. "The vajra-nature should be summoned" means performing the union; this is to be understood through the command of the Guru. "One will go to the realm of the Vajra-holder" means that upon the sheep-cart, one should place a sun mandala arising from the syllable *rāṃ*, and therein [place] the Vajra-holder arising from the syllable *hūṃ*.

The meaning is that, having generated the form and blessed the eyes and so forth, one should protect [the body] and lead it to the locations of the union and so on, and cause it to abide there. What is called "the yoga of self-blessing" (svādhiṣṭhāna-yoga) is the yoga of the completion stage (niṣpannakrama). Regarding the phrase "in the center of the heart," it refers to the junction where the two jewels are bound. "Vajra Nairātmya Ḍākinī... [and so forth].

"Action" refers to the visualization of a subtle jewel in the form of a *yoni* (vulva), which is the nature of Nairātmyā, arising from the complete transformation of the vajra. "The stable and the moving" refers to the wheel of the maṇḍala; some say it refers to the emission of the bodhicitta. "The limit of purity" means the limit of purification, which has become the central channel (*madhyamā*). "The net of conceptualization" refers to—

The objects of apprehension and the subjects of grasping. "Non-sentient" means that they are merely luminous clarity. "False" refers to the objects of apprehension and so forth. "Self" refers to the form of the afflictions. The "five hindrances" are sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt. All aspects...

"Omniscience" (*sarvajñatā*) refers to being skilled in all aspects. In order to refute that which is established from causes that are inconsistent with the result, it says "the thirty-two marks," and so forth. The meaning of this is the wheel of the maṇḍala that summarizes the five perfections (*pāramitā*) embraced by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

The meaning is that while the *svabhāva* (nature) is the means, emptiness alone—like the sphere of infinite space and so forth—will not lead to the attainment of peace. "Not true" means that when analyzed in terms of unity and plurality, it is merely an appearance. "Not false" refers to the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*.

It is because it is taught in various [scriptures]. "Not to be discarded" means that there is no nature of obscuration to be abandoned. "Not to be adopted" means that it does not produce what was previously non-existent. "The fist" (*khutsur*) refers to all the fingers being clenched together. "The lion’s ear" (*seng ge'i rna ba*) refers to the index and middle fingers being slightly bent.

‘Dod pa’ (kāma) means ‘to write’; ‘bo la’ (bola) means ‘gandharīṣa’; ‘sa li dza’ (sali-dza) means ‘khānadasa’; ‘ka tzor’ (katzoḥ) means ‘śati’. Regarding the phrase “this is the maṇḍala of the accumulations,” the word “this” (‘di) indicates the reason, because it is for the sake of amassing the accumulation of merit. “Vajrasattva” refers to the one generated by the syllable *hūṃ*. “De ru” (de ru) means...

"Padma'i sna rtse" means "the lotus jewel. "Dbyangs" refers to speech; the jewel therein is the natural radiance of the Buddha's voice. "Yid bzhin nor bu" refers to the vajra-jewel. Regarding the phrase "the syllable *phat* as the gateway of the jewel," it refers to a yellow *phat*. "The hand of the eye" means that from the back of the index finger, one uses the middle finger to grasp the tip of the index finger, forming the shape of an eye.

"Placed upon the palm" means it is positioned on top of the left hand. "The listening hand" refers to making the two hands resemble a banner and tongue, and then circling them completely. "The left hand should perform the circling" means that the right fist is held above the inverted left palm, with the thumb extended. "The vajra foot-step" refers to the single-pronged, three-pronged, and [multi-pronged] vajras.

Regarding the "Ten-Faced Manner" (*kha bcu pa'i tshul*), which is the *LNGA PA* and the various *Vajra-gatis*: it is the manner of making the ten fingers the tips by moving them [outward]. Furthermore, there are four types: the lion’s gait (*siṃha-gati*), the lion’s crouch (*siṃha-vikrānta*), the Vajrabhairava manner, and the snake-head manner. Regarding the term "variegated stalk" (*dbu gyi pa bkra bo*): it refers to the stalk and the variegated [stalk].

Having joined [the hands], one utters ordinary sounds. Furthermore, there are seven modes for producing sounds such as those of birth, and seven modes for producing sounds from instruments such as the lute (*vīṇā*). What is called "the mode of the *bhyiṅga* bird" refers to extending and raising the little fingers; these are the twelve [mudrās] beginning with the power of the Buddha (*buddhabala*). What is called "the second banner" refers to holding [the hands] like the thumb and little finger touching at their tips. The banner...

"Third" refers to performing the same action with both the thumb and the middle finger. This concludes the explanation of the fourteenth chapter from the *Detailed Exposition of Reality*, the Commentary on the Difficult Points of the *Vajrapañjara* of the Ḍākinīs.

Regarding "Kuru Kulle," this refers to the goddess Kuru Kulle; according to the oral instructions (*upadeśa*), she dwells in the midst of the eight charnel grounds, adorned with ornaments such as human bones, abiding in a dance accompanied by the *ardhaparyaṅka* posture. Regarding "Maṇi," this is the discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*), which is like a jewel of immense value. Why is it the discerning wisdom?

If it is asked, "Will this not then become accompanied by conceptualization? the word *padma* (lotus) is stated. The meaning is that, just as a lotus is not defiled by mud, that primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) is not defiled by the faults of conceptualization. For that very reason, *hūṃ phaṭ* is stated: *hūṃ* refers to the mind that is empty of subject and object; *phaṭ* refers to the shattering of discursive thought (*vikalpa*). *Mañju*.
*Badzra ya* means "name. *Mu* means the supreme mind of all Buddhas. *Hrīḥ* means casting down all Māras. *Śthriḥ*.

"Thus" (*iti*) means that by tearing asunder the jaws, he subdues those who are hateful, such as those in the heavens and the hells. "Vikṛtānana" means having a terrifying face with distorted features. The two pairs of *hūṃ* and *phaṭ* serve to eliminate aging and death. Regarding "mārīci," *māra* refers to the Māras, and *ci* means to suppress; thus, it refers to the suppression of the Māras.

*Gnon pas ma r'i rtsi'o* (The pressing [of the hand] is not for me). Regarding *Ba su dha ra*, it means "invocation. Regarding *Ba su brishṭi ni ba da ni*: *Ba su* refers to wealth such as jewels and so forth; *brishṭi* is the rain of those [jewels]. *Dzambhala* is the name. *Dza lendra ya* means that by giving water, he bestows sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). *Ma nī dha ra* means men and women.

It is called *Ratna* because it takes [the embryo] into the womb. *Vajra* means that by destroying the lower realms (*apāya*), it leads those who are terrified away from them like a thunderbolt. *Mahāpratisarā* means that it destroys and renders invisible those who have fallen into the great sufferings of hell and so forth. *Hūṃ Phaṭ* means that it destroys and causes [them] to fall. *Mahākālāya* means the name...

*Na au ba ha ri ā pa* means "to inflict harm upon those who cause injury to the Teaching. *Ya ti pra ti dnyā sma ra si* means "you have made a vow. *Kha kha* means "to cover" or "to conceal. *Khā hi khā hi* is explained as "to bestow. *Gṛhṇa gṛhṇa* is to be connected with "fever" (*jvara*) and so forth. *Bandha bandha*.

The phrase "zhes bya ba" (so-called) is to be connected with "mgrin pa zhags pa" (the neck is bound). "Da ha da ha" is to be connected with "intense blazing. "Ba tsa pa tsa" means that very same [practice], signifying that it should be performed as the third stage of the previously mentioned wheel of wrathful rites (*abhicāra*).

"Kṣaṇa" refers to *ānanda* (joy). Therein, "kṣaṇa" is *paramānanda* (supreme joy); "hetukṣaṇa" is *viramānanda* (special joy); and "svabhāva" is the nature of *sahajānanda* (innate joy). This very [innate joy] is also *mahāsukha* (great bliss), which is untainted bliss (*anāsravasukha*). *Viramānanda* is the beginning, *paramānanda* is the end, and "bhāva" refers to—

Regarding "the six, such as the *bala*," the phrase "Vajrasattva, the Perfect Buddha" is to be connected with the first [line]. "Dharma" refers to the causes of purification, such as generosity, which are rooted in the view of selflessness (*anātman*). "Samaya" consists of what is to be guarded and what is to be consumed. Regarding those, "guarding" refers to [avoiding] harm to the Three Jewels and so forth; "consuming" refers to eating the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*).

Regarding the statement "one should draw the maṇḍala," this means that one should constantly practice the three yogas: the maṇḍala of colored powders, the gaṇacakra, and meditative absorption (samādhi).

Regarding the phrase "the binding of mudrās should be abandoned," this refers to yogins of the completion stage who experience the bliss of Mahāmudrā, and not to beginners. For those [beginners], the very abandonment of binding mudrās would constitute a transgression. The phrase "maṇḍala and so forth" includes other physical movements by means of the word "and so forth. As for the actions of the body:

Regarding the phrase "should not be done," this refers to the abandonment of the activities of the three types of yoga. Among these, those who have attained some mastery over primordial wisdom (*jñāna*) cause boys and girls to cast lots and then perform the construction of mandalas and so forth. Those who have attained mastery over all primordial wisdoms perform the emanation and reabsorption of the mental mandala. As for those who have brought authentic primordial wisdom under their control...

By this, that very emanation mandala is to be shown as being similar to a reflected image and so forth. "One should not prostrate to those who are not masters" means that one does not bow before kings and others out of a desire for gain and the like.
"Guru" refers to those who teach mantra and so forth. "Elders" refers to the senior masters (*ācāryas*). The remainder refers to beginners, which is easy to understand.

He is one who possesses the yoga of the three daughters. Furthermore, he is endowed with the qualities of a teacher as previously described. He alone is the glorious Vajradhara because of his supreme service to the Holder of the Vajra; by him [the disciple] is duly consecrated, and not by others—meaning not by those whose vision of the supreme immutable is defiled by stains.

Regarding the phrase "empowered by the glorious Vajradhara" and so forth: a master who knows the ten suchnesses (*daśatattva*), is skilled in the ritual of drawing the mandala, abides in the commitments (*samaya*) and vows (*saṃvara*), is constantly endowed with the yoga of the three meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), and possesses all other qualities as previously described—such a master is called "Glorious Vajra" because he is extremely close to Vajradhara.
"O Grasper! One should perform the ritual of empowerment exactly as it is prescribed, and not otherwise."

"He has died"—this does not mean [he has died] in his own essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*), but rather that he is like a journey to a park, in the sense of being seen as a journey. "The station of the sky-farer" (*khecarīpada*) refers to one who has attained the vision of perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) because of the attainment of the unsurpassed state. "In Sukhāvatī" means in the completely pure world-system (*pariśuddhalokadhātu*) because of the attainment of sovereignty over the ten stages (*daśabhūmīśvaratva*). "By will" means that those who possess mastery over limited knowledge, by virtue of their mastery over birth, are born in whatever place they desire; this is the meaning. This applies even to beginners (*ādikarmika*).
Sometimes, by the power of karma, they go to the lower realms; there, it is certain from their vows that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas provide assistance through manifold skillful means.

Regarding the phrase "called *chi ba*," and so forth: "called *chi ba*" refers to that which is not authentic, such as going from grove to grove for the sake of sacrificial offerings. "The abode of *kha-spyod*" (the sky-farer) refers to those who have attained mastery over authentic primordial wisdom (*jñāna*); mastery over primordial wisdom is the attainment of the [enlightened] state. "Sukhāvatī" (the Land of Bliss) is the world-system of supreme joy.

"Then, he attains the sovereignty of the ten stages. Regarding the phrase "if he so desires," this refers to those who have attained mastery over some degree of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*); because they have attained mastery over rebirth, they will be born wherever they desire. Furthermore, even if beginners should go to the lower realms through the power of karma, they are followed by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas through various ritual methods.
"He causes [the disciple] to grasp [the bell], for the sake of obtaining the corresponding aspiration and empowerment.

Regarding the phrase "having placed the vajra-bell in the hand," this is merely an illustration; the remainder is easily understood. In this context, the meaning is as follows: having manifested [the disciple] in the form of one's own chosen deity, preceded by the invocation of the *jñānasattva*, and having performed the consecration of the eyes and so forth, one should recite the mantra garland many times.

The phrase "the vajra and bell are placed in the hands" is an elliptical expression; in the same manner, other [implements] should also be applied accordingly. In this regard, their meaning is as follows: having first invited the wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*) into the form of one's chosen deity, and having consecrated the eyes and so forth, one should recite the mantra garland many times.

Regarding "by means of the application of the vajra-pit" (*vajrakuṇḍaprayogeṇa*): having drawn the maṇḍala according to the rules and performed the maṇḍala-sādhana and so forth; having consecrated [the disciple] with the water, crown, vajra, lord, name, and vase empowerments; having performed worship, praise, the tasting of nectar (*amṛtāsvāda*), and so on; and having recited the mantra many times; one should [visualize] the fire as Vajrasattva or one's own chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) within its heart according to the rules.

Having completed the circle of the retinue and having dismissed the deceased as the *jñānasattva*, one should resolve that his *samayasattva* becomes of one flavor with the circle of the retinue; this is the meaning of "one should perform the consecration. If this ritual action is not performed, then there would be the destruction of the stūpa.

"By means of the application of the vajra hearth" means that, having drawn the mandala exactly as it is, and having preceded this with the mandala-sādhana and so forth, one confers the empowerments of water, crown, vajra, lord, name, and vase; then, having performed the offerings, praises, and the tasting of the nectar (*amṛta*), one recites many mantras, and then—

Having generated Vajrasattva at the heart, or one’s own meditational deity (iṣṭadevatā) together with their maṇḍala retinue, [one should] merge them as one with the wisdom maṇḍala. Visualizing that they have entered into a state of equanimity, one should perform the purification by burning in the site of the peaceful fire offering (*śāntihoma*). If one does not do so, it will result in the very destruction of the stūpa.
The commentary on the fifteenth chapter of the *Tattvaviṣadā*, a detailed analysis (*pañjikā*) of the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*. || 0 ||
From the *Extensive Commentary on Reality*, the difficult commentary on the *Vajrapañjara* of the Ḍākinīs, this is the explanation of the fifteenth chapter.
Having attained some degree of awakening through service at the feet of the Guru,
I have explained this noble tantra in a manner corresponding to my own capacity.
By the abundant merit that I have acquired through this pure [deed],
may the multitude of beings not be deprived of the bliss of tranquility.
By whatever merit has been gathered from unraveling this great,
vast, and difficult-to-comprehend King of Tantras through the instructions obtained from the feet of the Guru—
by that stainless and abundant mass of virtue, may [all beings] attain [enlightenment].
"May the multitudes of living beings proceed upon the path free from suffering.
Thus ends the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara-pañjikā* titled *Tattvaviṣadā*, composed by Mahāmatideva. Om. Om. Om.

The *Detailed Commentary on the Reality* (*Tattvavistara-nāma-ḍākinīvajrapañjara-pañjikā*), composed by the great master known as Devakulamahāmati, is hereby complete. It was translated, edited, and finalized by the great Indian preceptor Gayadhara and the Tibetan translator 'Gos Lhas btsas.
